Les avis divergent sur les sept redites. Omar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra et la majorité des exégètes, dont al-Qurtubi et al-Razi, y voient la sourate al-Fatiha. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr et Mujahid les identifient aux sept longues sourates, de la Vache à Jonas, tandis que Tawus et Abu Malik désignent l'ensemble du Coran et que Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam y voit sept genres de sens. Quant à « fixer le regard », Ibn 'Uyayna en fait une invitation à se suffire du Coran, tandis qu'Ibn 'Abbas y voit le désir du bien d'autrui.

Les « partageurs » (al-muqtasimin) sont identifiés par Ibn 'Abbas et Sa'id ibn Jubayr aux gens du Livre qui ont divisé leur Écriture, et par Qatada et al-Farra' aux Quraychites qui qualifiaient le Coran de magie, de poésie ou de divination. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari rapportent aussi diverses causes de révélation, que d'autres jugent faibles.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de déclarer qu'il est le messager d'avertissement clair, qui met en garde les hommes contre le châtiment de Dieu s'ils persistent dans le déni, de la même manière que Dieu a fait descendre un châtiment sur les peuples précédents. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens de l'avertissement explicite, et sur la fonction de comparaison de la particule « kamā », même s'ils divergent sur l'objet sous-entendu de l'action d'annoncer. Quant aux « muqtasimūn », les avis sont multiples : Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid et Qatāda, dans l'une de leurs transmissions, y voient les gens du Livre, juifs et chrétiens, qui ont séparé leur Écriture en parties, croyant à une partie et rejetant l'autre ; al-Farrāʾ et Qatāda y voient un groupe de Quraychites qui se répartirent les accès de La Mecque lors du pèlerinage pour détourner les gens du Prophète ; Ibn Zayd les identifie aux gens de Ṣāliḥ qui se sont juré de le tuer la nuit ; Abū Ḥayyān et d'autres rapportent encore d'autres opinions. Pour le mot « ʿiḍīn », Ibn ʿAbbās et al-Ḍaḥḥāk y voient le pluriel de « ʿuḍw », c'est-à-dire des parties et des morceaux, tandis que Qatāda et al-Kisāʾī le rattachent à la calomnie, et ʿIkrima ainsi que al-Farrāʾ le rapprochent de la magie selon le parler de Quraysh. Le verset vient après l'ordre de ne pas s'attrister pour les mécréants et d'abaisser son aile envers les croyants, l'avertissement venant ainsi confirmer la mission du Prophète et annoncer le sort de ceux qui démentent.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de déclarer aux gens qu'il est un avertisseur clair, et que son avertissement est semblable au châtiment que Dieu a fait descendre sur les « muqtasimin ». Les commentateurs divergent fortement sur l'identité de ces derniers. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan et Ibn Zayd, suivis par al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, y voient les gens du Livre, juifs et chrétiens, qui ont cru en une partie de leurs Écritures et rejeté l'autre en la divisant ; 'Ikrima rapporte que certains se la partageaient par moquerie, disant « cette sourate est à moi ». Qatada, al-Farra' et d'autres y voient des notables de Quraysh qui se répartirent les accès de La Mecque à la saison du pèlerinage pour détourner les gens du Prophète, en le qualifiant de sorcier, de poète ou de devin. Ibn Zayd désigne le peuple de Salih qui se jura de le tuer, et al-Akhfash les hommes liés par des serments. Quant à « 'idin », Ibn 'Abbas et al-Dahhak y voient le sens de morceaux ou de parts, tandis que Qatada, 'Ikrima et al-Farra' le rattachent à la calomnie ou à la magie. Le point commun est que ceux qui ont fragmenté le Coran ou le Livre et l'ont qualifié de manières contradictoires méritent le châtiment, et que le Prophète n'est pas le seul à subir ce genre d'épreuve.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète de déclarer qu'il est l'avertisseur clair, mettant en garde contre un châtiment semblable à celui qui frappa les peuples qui ont traité leurs messagers de menteurs. Les commentateurs divergent sur l'identité des « muqtasimin » (ceux qui se sont partagé). Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid et al-Hasan y voient les gens du Livre, juifs et chrétiens, qui ont cru en une partie de leur Écriture et rejeté l'autre. Selon 'Ikrima, il s'agit de gens qui se moquaient du Coran en disant chacun : « Cette sourate est à moi ». Qatada et Muqatil y voient des notables de Qurayš que al-Walid ibn al-Mughira envoya aux accès de La Mecque pendant la saison du pèlerinage pour détourner les gens du Prophète, en qualifiant celui-ci tantôt de sorcier, tantôt de poète, tantôt de devin. Ibn Zayd y voit le peuple de Salih qui avait juré de le tuer de nuit, interprétation que Ibn Atiyya juge difficilement compatible avec la suite. Quant à « 'idin », pluriel de « 'ida », la lecture la plus répandue est « partager en morceaux » : ils ont fragmenté le Coran et proféré des jugements contradictoires à son sujet. Al-Farra' et al-Kisa'i l'ont rattaché à la racine 'd-h, la calomnie ou la magie. Al-Tabari préfère appliquer le verset aux polythéistes de Qurayš, vu le contexte de la sourate. Sur « Par ton Seigneur, Nous les interrogerons tous », Abu al-'Aliya et Mujahid y voient une question sur le témoignage de la profession de foi, tandis que d'autres l'entendent de toutes les actions. Dieu ordonne ensuite de proclamer ouvertement ce qui est commandé et de se détourner des associateurs, car Il suffit à son Prophète contre les moqueurs. Le passage s'achève par l'ordre de glorifier Dieu, de se prosterner et d'adorer jusqu'à la mort.

Dieu jure par Son Seigneurie, comme l'expliquent les exégètes, qu'Il interrogera le jour de la Résurrection tous ces contempteurs sur ce qu'ils faisaient, interrogatoire qui est à la fois réprimande et menace. Les commentateurs divergent sur la portée de ce questionnement et sur ceux qu'il vise. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya et Ibn Zayd estiment qu'il concerne tous les hommes, croyants comme mécréants, tandis que d'autres y voient un interrogatoire réservé aux incroyants et aux moqueurs. Quant aux « muqtasimun », al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir les identifient aux Gens du Livre qui ont divisé leurs Écritures, croyant en une partie et rejetant l'autre, Ibn Kathir s'appuyant sur un hadith rapporté dans les deux Sahih ; al-Farra' et al-Suddi y voient plutôt les notables de Quraych qui se partagèrent les accès de La Mecque pour détourner les gens du Prophète. Az-Zamakhshari et d'autres rapportent que certains dirent du Coran que c'était de la poésie, d'autres de la magie. Le terme « 'idin » est expliqué par la division en parties, ou par le sens de calomnie ou de magie selon les lexicographes. Ils s'accordent sur le caractère de réprimande et de jugement de cet interrogatoire, tout en discutant de la contradiction apparente avec le verset 55:39. Ibn Jarir et Ibn Kathir rapportent, d'après Anas, Ibn 'Umar et Mujahid, que la question porte sur la déclaration « Il n'y a de dieu que Allah » ; Ibn al-Qayyim y voit la sincérité dans son accomplissement. Les exégètes ne tranchent pas nettement entre ces lectures.

Ce verset rapporte le serment divin : Dieu interrogera tous les hommes, le Jour de la Résurrection, sur ce qu'ils faisaient ici-bas. Les commentateurs expliquent cette interrogation de plusieurs façons voisines. La plupart rapportent qu'il s'agit d'être interrogé sur la profession de foi « Il n'y a de divinité que Dieu », comme le transmettent Anas, Ibn Umar et Mujahid ; Ibn Kathir et d'autres notent que ce sens est attribué au Prophète par la voie d'Anas, tout en signalant qu'une version la rapporte comme parole de compagnon. Abu al-Aliya affirme que les hommes seront interrogés sur deux choses : ce qu'ils adoraient et ce qu'ils ont répondu aux messagers. Ibn Abbas et ceux qui le suivent précisent que cette question est une réprimande et non une enquête, puisque Dieu connaît déjà tous les actes ; c'est aussi l'avis de Qutrub, qui distingue cette question de celle niée dans la sourate Ar-Rahman. Ibn Abbas y voit un Jour aux étapes multiples, selon 'Ikrima. Al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi étendent le sens à toutes les actions, de paroles, d'actes et d'omissions. Al-Qurtubi conclut à la généralité de la question pour les croyants comme pour les mécréants. Ibn Juzayy résume la conciliation : la question affirmée vise le jugement et le reproche, la question niée vise l'enquête pure. Tous s'accordent sur le caractère de menace adressée à ceux qui ont nié la révélation et morcelé le Coran.

Ce verset ordonne au Prophète ﷺ de proclamer ouvertement ce qui lui est commandé et de se détourner des associateurs sans se laisser détourner par leurs moqueries. Le sens du mot « faṣda‘ » fait l'objet de plusieurs lectures. Ibn ‘Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi et Abu al-Su‘ud y voient la proclamation et l'exécution de l'ordre. Mujahid l'entend comme la récitation du Coran à voix haute dans la prière. Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, al-Nasafi et Ibn Juzayy y lisent une séparation entre le vrai et le faux. Abu Hayyan et al-Shawkani relèvent que « mâ » peut être relatif, désignant les prescriptions, ou verbal, désignant l'ordre lui-même.

Les commentateurs rapportent généralement que le Prophète était resté discret jusqu'à la révélation de ce verset, puis qu'il sortit avec ses compagnons. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi citent aussi les récits sur la révélation qui suivent, où le texte condamne d'abord les associateurs, sans que ces récits soient présentés comme un avis tranché de chacun.

Sur la question de l'abrogation, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Qurtubi rapportent que « a‘ridh » a été abrogé par les versets du combat, tandis qu'al-Razi, Ibn ‘Atiyya et al-Shinqiti jugent cet avis faible ou incomplet et tiennent que le verbe signifie seulement ne pas se soucier d'eux. Ibn ‘Ashur précise qu'il s'agit d'ignorer leurs moqueries et leurs attaques, et non leur appel à l'islam.

Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que Dieu a suffi au Prophète contre les moqueurs, et que ces derniers périrent. Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi racontent comment cinq chefs de Quraysh furent châtiés. Ibn Kathir et Ibn Sa‘di concluent que le verset appelle à la patience, à la louange et à la prière, et que l'expression « jusqu'à ce que te vienne la certitude » désigne la mort selon la majorité des exégètes.

Dans ce verset, Dieu s'adresse à son Prophète ﷺ pour lui ordonner de proclamer clairement ce qui lui est commandé, de ne craindre que Dieu et de se détourner des polythéistes sans s'en soucier, car Dieu lui a suffi contre ceux qui le raillaient. Les commentateurs s'accordent à désigner par les moqueurs (al-mustahzi'in) quelques notables de Quraych, que la plupart comptent au nombre de cinq : al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib et al-Harith ibn Qays ibn al-Talatila. Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir rapportent qu'ils périrent avant Badr, frappés par diverses calamités. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi et d'autres citent des récits variés, transmis par Ibn Ishaq, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima ou Muqatil, qui divergent sur leur nombre et sur la manière dont ils moururent. Al-Shi'bi en compte sept et y ajoute Habbar ibn al-Aswad, ce qu'Ibn 'Atiyya tient pour une erreur, Habbar s'étant converti le jour de la conquête de La Mecque. Al-Razi estime que ces détails ne sont pas nécessaires et qu'il suffit de savoir qu'ils étaient puissants. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi, en revanche, rapportent le sort de chacun. Quant à l'expression "jusqu'à ce que te vienne la certitude", la majorité des exégètes, dont Ibn Zayd, Mujahid et al-Hasan, y voient la mort, tandis que Shajara la comprend comme la victoire.

Ce verset rapporte que Dieu a suffi à Son Prophète ﷺ contre ceux qui le raillaient. La plupart des commentateurs désignent cinq notables de Qurayш : al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, Abu Zam'a, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth et al-Harith ibn al-Talatila, qui périrent avant Badr, chacun par un accident ou une maladie que les récits détaillent. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent ces récits, tandis que al-Sha'bi et Ibn Abi Bazza parlent de sept personnes, et qu'Ibn Juzayy estime que le sens le plus probable vise ceux qui périrent à Mecque avant l'hégire, alors que d'autres pensent aux tués de Badr comme Abu Jahl. Le verset se termine par une menace : ceux qui associent à Dieu un autre dieu sauront ce qui les attend, et les commentateurs y voient un avertissement qui vise tout polythéiste. Al-Mawardi cite plusieurs sens du verbe « sadda'a » (proclamer ouvertement), et al-Tabari comme Ibn Kathir y voient l'ordre de transmettre le message sans crainte. Al-Razi et Abu al-Su'ud expliquent que la mention de l'associationnisme console le Prophète en montrant que ses adversaires ont commis un péché plus grave encore que la moquerie. Al-Sha'rawi précise que le mot « sawfa » couvre plusieurs étapes : certains adversaires finissent par se repentir, à l'image de 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl. Les commentaires s'accordent donc sur un sens clair : une consolation pour le Prophète et une menace différée pour les polythéistes, dont la fin sera connue dans ce monde et dans l'au-delà.

Dieu informe Son Prophète Muhammad ﷺ qu'Il sait combien son cœur est oppressé par ce que disent les païens : démentis, moqueries et critiques du Coran. Il lui ordonne alors de se réfugier dans la glorification de son Seigneur, la louange et la prière, et de persévérer dans l'adoration jusqu'à ce que lui vienne « la certitude », c'est-à-dire la mort selon la grande majorité des commentateurs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent que le mot yaqin désigne la mort, en s'appuyant sur les propos de Salim, Mujahid et Qatada. Ibn Kathir en tire que l'adoration reste obligatoire tant que la raison demeure, et réfute l'idée que la connaissance de Dieu dispenserait de l'obligation. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Atiyya estiment que le terme désigne la certitude de la mort plutôt que la mort elle-même, et que la limite fixée signifie toute la durée de la vie ; Ibn Atiyya envisage aussi qu'il s'agisse de la victoire promise. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que la glorification accompagnée de louange est la déclaration de la transcendance divine avec remerciement, et que le prosternement désigne la prière. Ils citent le hadith selon lequel le Prophète ﷺ, lorsqu'une affaire l'affligeait, se tournait vers la prière. Quant à la cause de l'oppression, al-Tabari et d'autres y voient le démenti, tandis qu'al-Razi et d'autres y voient la moquerie ; al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi notent que le « cœur » est désigné par la poitrine. La verse se rattache aux moqueurs que Dieu a rendus impuissants, dont les commentateurs racontent la mort, même si leurs noms et leur nombre varient selon les récits.

Dans ce verset, Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ, après avoir rappelé que son cœur se resserre devant le rejet et les moqueries de son peuple, de se réfugier auprès de son Seigneur par la glorification, la louange et la prière, afin que Dieu le délivre de ce qui l'afflige, puis de persévérer dans l'adoration jusqu'à ce que vienne la certitude, c'est-à-dire la mort. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le « prosternement » désigne ici la prière, et que la glorification signifie la déclaration de la pureté de Dieu et la louange de Lui. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir rapportent que la glorification peut se dire par la formule « Gloire à Dieu et louange à Lui », et que les prosternés sont les fidèles en prière ou les humbles. La majorité entend par « la certitude » la mort, comme le rapportent Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada et Ibn Zayd, tandis que Shajara et Ibn Juzayy, cités par al-Mawardi et Ibn al-Jawzi, y voient la victoire promise. Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi en tirent l'obligation de l'adoration tant que la raison demeure, et réfutent ceux qui prétendent que la certitude est la connaissance, ce qui dispenserait de l'obligation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi expliquent que la prière apaise l'angoisse, et Ibn Ashur, comme al-Shinqiti, relève que l'ordre de glorifier Dieu après la gêne du cœur montre que la prière est un moyen de dissiper cette peine. Al-Jaza'iri en déduit la légitimité de la prière de besoin. Quant à savoir si ce passage comporte une prosternation de récitation, la plupart des savants le nient, tandis qu'al-Naqqash et d'autres l'ont admise.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de persévérer dans l'adoration de son Seigneur jusqu'à ce que lui vienne al-yaqin, c'est-à-dire la mort. Selon la majorité des commentateurs, cela signifie que l'adoration reste obligatoire tant que l'on vit, sans interruption ne serait-ce qu'un instant. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, Salim ibn Abd Allah et Ibn Zayd expliquent ainsi le terme yaqin par la mort, et al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir s'appuient sur le récit de Umm al-Ala au sujet de la mort de Uthman ibn Maz'un. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya et al-Shawkani rapportent une autre lecture, selon laquelle le yaqin serait la victoire promise au Prophète, transmise par Shajara et Ibn Bahr. Al-Zajjaj, al-Razi et Ibn al-Jawzi font remarquer que la mention d'un terme indique la continuité : un ordre d'adorer sans limite pourrait être accompli par un seul acte. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di et Ibn Ashur en tirent que l'obligation subsiste tant que la raison est présente, et que la prière se fait debout, assis ou couché selon ses capacités. Ibn Kathir et al-Shinqiti rejettent comme égarée l'interprétation qui ferait du yaqin la connaissance de Dieu, laquelle ferait tomber la charge religieuse. Ce passage s'inscrit dans la suite de la sourate : après l'appel à proclamer le message et à se détourner des polythéistes, le remède au chagrin est la glorification et la prostration, puis la constance dans l'adoration jusqu'à la fin de la vie.

This verse states that the disjointed letters at the opening of the surah (Alif, Lam, Ra) are verses of this perfect Book and of a Qur'an that makes things clear, distinguishing truth from falsehood and the lawful from the unlawful. The commentators agree that the demonstrative "those" refers to the verses of this surah or to the whole Book. They differ on what "the Book" means: al-Tabari, citing Qatada and Mujahid, takes it to be the Torah and the Gospel and the scriptures that came before the Qur'an, while Ibn Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Qur'an itself, the two names being joined to stress its greatness. Al-Mawardi gives three meanings of "clear": that its inimitability is manifest, that it separates truth from falsehood, and that it separates the lawful from the unlawful. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud note that the indefinite form of "a Qur'an" is used for emphasis.

The next verse, "Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims," raises the question of when this wish will occur. Al-Dahhak says it will come at the moment of death; Mujahid says it will come when the terrors of the Day of Resurrection are seen; Ibn Abbas, Anas, Ibn Mas'ud and most exegetes say it will come when sinful Muslims are brought out of the Fire. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari favour this last view, relying on transmitted reports, and al-Razi supports it too. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain the word "perhaps" (rubama) as signalling rarity, while others take it as emphasis; al-Razi reads it as a rhetorical device to stress the certainty of the regret. Ibn Atiyya notes that Abu Hayyan treats the particle as a preposition.

The following verse tells the Prophet to leave the disbelievers to eat and enjoy themselves, with hope distracting them. Ibn Kathir sees this as a severe warning. Ibn Atiyya holds that this permission of leniency was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas Abu Hayyan reads it as an order to shun the disbelievers rather than to fight them.

This verse says that those who disbelieved will at some point wish they had been Muslims, a wish that comes too late. The commentators differ on when this wish occurs. Al-Dahhak places it at the moment of witnessing in this world, when guidance becomes clear from error; Mujahid and Qatada place it on the Day of Resurrection; and many, including Ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Mujahid, Abu al-Aliya and Ibrahim, link it to the moment when God brings sinful believers out of the Fire, citing the report of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Ibn Abbas also relates that God keeps admitting people to Paradise and granting intercession until He says that whoever was a Muslim should enter Paradise, and then this wish arises. Scholars note that 'rubba' originally signifies fewness, so explanations vary: al-Zamakhshari sees an expression giving the opposite of the literal sense to emphasise intensity, while al-Razi and others suggest the torment so preoccupies them that such wishes come only occasionally. Most exegetes read the passage as a warning to the polytheists, with the Prophet told to leave them to eat, enjoy themselves and be distracted by hope until they learn their fate. The final verse notes that every community has a fixed term in the Book, which it neither precedes nor outlasts.

The commentators read this verse as a address to the Prophet ﷺ: leave the idolaters to eat and enjoy their worldly life, and let the hope of long years distract them from obeying God and preparing for the afterlife; they will soon know the outcome of what they have done. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, take it as a threat and a warning, understanding eating and enjoying as the pleasure of cattle, heedless of the end, and hope as greed for this world, the wish for a long life and turning away from the hereafter.

Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur stress that the purpose is to cut off any hope of their faith, so that further urging them is futile; the command to leave them then conveys despair of their reform. The scholars differ on abrogation: al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, and others after them, say the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Shawkani, al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur consider that no abrogation is needed, since it belongs to a Meccan context affirming that admonition cannot guide. Al-Razi cites it, for the Sunni position, as evidence that God may turn people away from faith; the Mu'tazilites reply that it is a threat, not a permission.

The commentators agree that the threat will be fulfilled in this world through humiliation, death and captivity, and in the next through punishment, and that the outcome is certain. On the moral level, the verse teaches that pursuing pleasure and long hopes are not traits of believers; al-Qurtubi relates a saying of al-Hasan: "Whoever prolongs his hope does evil in his deeds."

This verse states that God never destroyed a town without it having a fixed, known term written for it, from which its destruction can neither come early nor be delayed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God does not destroy a people until the proof has been established against them and their term has ended, and that the verse is a warning to the people of Mecca to abandon polytheism and obstinacy. On what destruction means, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as the punishment of total annihilation, while al-Razi holds that it covers both that punishment and natural death, though he considers annihilation the closer meaning because it is the stronger deterrent. As for the Known Book, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi take it to be what is recorded in the Preserved Tablet, al-Mawardi allows either a fixed term or an inevitable decree, and al-Hasan reports that it refers to a messenger and a scripture sent to a community before its punishment. The commentators also differ on the grammar of the waw in the phrase about the town having a book: al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa treat the clause as a qualifier, whereas Abu Hayyan and Ibn Malik reject this and read it as a circumstantial clause. Despite these differences, they agree that the term cannot be advanced or postponed and that one should not be deceived by the respite granted. Al-Hasan adds that whoever prolongs his hopes spoils his deeds.

This verse states that God never destroyed a community without first fixing a determined term for it: no people goes ahead of its appointed time, nor falls behind it. The commentators read it as a warning to the Meccan disbelievers, urging them to take heed of God's established practice with earlier peoples. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi agree that the destruction meant is the total annihilation sent upon peoples who reject their messengers, and that the 'known Book' is the decreed term. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer that the phrase may mean either a fixed term or an inevitable decree, and al-Mawardi adds that the people neither die before the punishment, and so find rest, nor are spared it. Al-Hasan gives a third reading: no nation is punished before its messenger and its scripture have come to it. Al-Razi holds that the destruction may refer to annihilation, to death, or to both together, and he draws from the verse the conclusion that every death happens at its appointed time. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a reminder not to be deceived by respite. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi discuss the grammar, explaining that the clause after the exception is a qualifying clause whose waw strengthens its attachment to the noun. Al-Qurtubi notes that 'min' here is an empty connecting particle. Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Sa'di emphasise that this divine law does not change and that every fall comes at its set hour.

This verse records the words of the disbelievers addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in mockery: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely mad!" followed by the demand: "Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are truthful?" The commentators agree that the "Reminder" is the Qur'an and that the speech is sarcastic, since those who truly believed it had been sent down would not call its bearer mad. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the demand for angels meant that they should witness to his truthfulness. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi give several meanings of "truth" in God's reply: revelation, punishment, or the taking of souls at death. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya explain that angels descend only for a just purpose, and that their coming would bring immediate punishment with no respite. As for the phrase "We surely guard it", most exegetes, including Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, take the pronoun as referring to the Qur'an, which God preserves from distortion and addition. Others, including al-Farra' and some of the exegetes quoted by al-Tabari, take it as referring to the Prophet, whom God protects from his enemies. Several commentators, including Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir, see in the passage a consolation for the Prophet, since earlier messengers were mocked in the same way.

This verse records the mockery of the polytheists towards the Prophet ﷺ: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are truly mad!" They then ask why he does not bring the angels to bear witness to his truthfulness, if he is sincere. The commentators agree that "lawma" means "why not" and expresses urging. Their aim is that the angels should attest to the prophetic mission or come to punish the deniers, as angels came to earlier nations. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that "lawma" can also mean the prevention of one thing by the existence of another, and they cite a line of Ibn Muqbil. The recitations differ: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ma tanazzalu al-mala'ikatu", while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "ma nunazzilu al-mala'ikata". God's reply, "We send down the angels only with truth", is explained by most as meaning that the angels descend only as divine wisdom requires. Mujahid takes truth to mean the message and punishment, al-Hasan takes it to mean punishment, and Ibn al-Jawzi takes it to mean the taking of souls at death. Al-Razi and others note that their descent would mean destruction without delay. All agree that "We sent down the Reminder, and We are its guardians" answers their taunt. Most hold that the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the Reminder, meaning it is protected from alteration, while another view takes it to refer to the Prophet, who is protected from his enemies.

This verse states that angels descend only with truth, and that the disbelievers who demanded their coming as witnesses to the Prophet would not be given respite once they appeared. Mujahid understands the truth as prophethood and punishment, al-Hasan as punishment if they do not believe, Ibn al-Sa'ib as the taking of souls at death, and al-Mawardi as the Quran. The commentators agree that the verse answers the challenge of the disbelievers and that the sending of angels follows divine wisdom. Al-Zamakhshari argues there is no wisdom in having the angels visible to all, since belief would then be forced, while al-Baydawi notes that God did not wish to hasten punishment for those whom He knew would believe or whose descendants would. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link the passage to the earlier nations who asked for signs and were destroyed when those signs came. As for the words 'We are its guardians', most exegetes, including Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir, take the pronoun as referring to the Quran, protected from alteration, whereas al-Farra' and al-Razi also report a reading that refers it to the Prophet, protected from his enemies, while noting that the Quran is closer to the context.

This verse states that God Himself sent down the Reminder, meaning the Quran, in reply to the mockery of the disbelievers who had called the Prophet ﷺ a madman to whom the Reminder was supposedly sent. The commentators agree that the Reminder is the Quran and that the emphatic form with inna and nahnu conveys certainty and majesty. As for the promised preservation, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain it as protection against any addition of falsehood or removal of truth that devils might attempt, citing the verse that falsehood cannot reach it from before or behind. Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Baydawi extend it to protection against distortion and alteration, noting that God took charge of the text itself, unlike earlier scriptures entrusted to their custodians. Al-Razi adds that the preservation may also rest on the Quran's inimitable composition, which would make any change immediately visible even to children. Al-Hasan understood it as preservation until the Day of Recompense. Some scholars held that the pronoun in lahu refers to the Prophet, who is guarded from his enemies, but most preferred that it refers to the Reminder, which fits the context more closely.

God consoles His Prophet ﷺ by reminding him that messengers were sent before him to the factions of earlier peoples, and that whenever a messenger came to a people they mocked him, just as the Meccan polytheists mock him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'the factions of the ancients' means the earlier nations, while al-Mawardi notes that the word may mean factions or tribes, and al-Hasan defines a shi'a as a group united on one doctrine. On 'We thread it into the hearts of the criminals' the commentators differ: Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij take it to mean mockery, denial or polytheism, with al-Hasan also understanding the Qur'an itself entering their hearts rejected, whereas Ibn Zayd says God misguided them and withheld faith from them. As for 'the way of the ancients has passed', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as the punishment of 'Ad and Thamud, al-Mawardi considers ruin or disbelief after miracles, and Qatada understands God's dealings with past nations. Al-Razi lists the reasons ignorant people mock prophets: dislike of obligations, attachment to inherited ways, the poverty of the messenger, and God's abandonment. Al-Tabari stresses that the verse comforts the Prophet by showing that his trial is not unprecedented. The commentators do not choose between these readings and present them as all possible.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that the pattern among earlier peoples was the same: He sent messengers to the groups and nations of the past, and whenever a messenger came to a people they met him with mockery. The commentators read this as consolation for the Prophet facing the ridicule of the Quraysh. On the word shiya', al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas and Qatada render it as peoples, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari as groups, while Ibn Atiyya understands it as factions gathered around a leader or doctrine. On the next verse, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God places denial in the hearts of the wrongdoers, who do not believe; Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan take this to mean polytheism, while Ibn Zayd and Qatada see it as God leading them astray. Ibn al-Qayyim, reflecting on the pronoun, holds that it refers to the Quran: God makes it enter their hearts by rejecting it, so that the proof stands against them. Al-Razi lists the reasons that lead the ignorant to mock prophets: the burden of obligations, abandoning inherited beliefs, the poverty of the messenger, and divine abandonment. All agree that the phrase about the way of the earlier peoples having passed is a warning to Mecca, recalling the punishment that struck nations who rejected their prophets. Ibn Kathir adds that the passage calls the Prophet to patience.

This verse states that God causes denial, rejection and mockery of the messenger to enter the hearts of the guilty among the Prophet's contemporaries, just as He did with earlier peoples who treated their messengers the same way, so they do not believe in the Quran or in the Prophet. The commentators differ on what the pronouns refer to. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij take the object to be polytheism, denial or mockery, whereas az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, and al-Hasan in one report, take it to be the Reminder, that is the Quran, which enters their hearts rejected and ridiculed. Az-Zamakhshari compares it to a request made to a miser that is turned down. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests combining the two readings, while al-Mawardi lists several possible referents, namely the messenger, the Quran or the punishment. As for the phrase about the custom of the ancients having passed, most read it as God's established practice of destroying those who deny, a warning to the people of Mecca, while Ibn Juraij understands it as the conduct of those peoples themselves. Several scholars, including Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi, use the verse as proof against the Qadariyya and the Mu'tazila, since the act is attributed to God. At-Tabari and others place it within the consolation of the Prophet for the mockery he endured.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of the wrongdoers, meaning the idolaters of Mecca, who do not believe in the Quran or the Prophet ﷺ. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the pronoun in 'We cause it to enter' refers to denial, to association, or to mockery, a view shared by al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij, so that this rejection enters their hearts and prevents them from believing. Al-Mawardi lists several possible meanings, including that God punishes those who persist in denial after the signs they asked for have come. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take the pronoun to refer to the Reminder, the Quran, which is cast into their hearts rejected and mocked, though al-Baydawi calls this reading grammatically weak. Al-Razi rejects the Mu'tazili interpretation and argues that God creates falsehood in the hearts of disbelievers, which he says was the view of earlier exegetes such as Ibn Abbas. As for 'the way of the earlier peoples', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as the destruction that struck nations who called their prophets liars, such as 'Ad and Thamud. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy connect the passage to a warning addressed to Quraysh. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse carries an implicit warning, since the fate of those peoples is well known. Most commentators therefore see the passage as a consolation to the Prophet and a threat to his contemporaries.

This verse describes the stubbornness of the Meccan disbelievers: even if God opened a gate in the sky and they climbed through it in daylight, seeing wonders with their own eyes, they would say their sight had been dazzled and that they were people under magic. The commentators agree that the passage warns the Quraysh and consoles the Prophet ﷺ over their mockery. They differ on who is climbing. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the angels, whom the disbelievers see plainly, while al-Hasan and Qatada take it to be the disbelievers themselves, a view al-Tabari judges less sound. The meaning of "sukkirat" also varies. Mujahid and Ibn Kathir say "blocked", al-Tabari settles on "seized and dimmed", Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala and Abu 'Ubayda relate it to the blurring of drunkenness, al-Kalbi says "blinded", and Ibn Zayd compares it to a drunk who no longer understands. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the lighter reading means "held back", like a stream that is dammed. Ibn Atiyya observes that "zallu" indicates the act happening by day. Despite these lexical differences, the commentators agree on the lesson: no sign benefits someone who has chosen to refuse.

This verse says that if the stubborn idolaters were given an open gate in the sky and saw the angels ascending and descending through it in broad daylight, they would still not believe, but would say that their eyes had been dazzled or clouded and that they had been bewitched. The commentators differ on who ascends. Al-Hasan and Qatada, followed by al-Mawardi, take it to be the disbelievers themselves who climb, while Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak, and al-Tabari in one of his views, take it to be the angels, whom the idolaters would witness. On the word suckkirat, most readers use the doubled form, and Ibn Kathir the single form. Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Qatada explain it as blocked or seized, al-Hasan as bewitched, al-Kalbi as blinded. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari link it more to intoxication or to the stilling of the wind, so that the sight is confused as a drunkard's is. Al-Tabari concludes that their eyes were seized and bewitched so that they do not see things as they truly are. Ibn Kathir reads the verse as a portrait of the obstinacy of Quraysh, whom Ibn Jarir identifies as the speakers. Al-Zamakhshari argues that "innama" here restricts the claim to a mere dazzling of the eyes. Al-Alusi and al-Razi add that these people understood the Qur'an and its inimitability, yet remained obstinate.

This verse states that God placed great structures, the buruj, in the sky and adorned the heavens with them for those who look at them. The commentators agree that these signs demonstrate God's power and wisdom and invite reflection. They differ, however, on the meaning of buruj. Mujahid, Qatada, Abu Salih and al-Tabari take it to mean the stars, while Ibn Abbas and Ali ibn Isa, as reported by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand the stations of the sun and moon, the twelve zodiacal signs. Atiyya al-Awfi describes them as palaces with guards, and al-Hasan and Qatada speak of large stars. Regarding the protection of the sky from devils, Ibn Abbas holds that a meteor burns the devil without killing him, whereas al-Hasan says it kills him. Several scholars, including al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, explain that the protection intensified at the birth of Jesus and then at the mission of the Prophet, and they differ on whether the shooting stars were known before Islam. Al-Baydawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi stress the reflective purpose of the verse, which calls the one who looks upward to consider the Creator.

The commentators explain that God protected the heaven from every accursed devil, meaning one who is driven away and cast out, so that he cannot draw near it or meddle in its affairs. God made an exception for the one who snatches a fleeting hearing of the heavenly news: a clear flaming star then pursues him, burning, wounding or disabling him. There is wide agreement on the basic sense of being pelted away and driven off, though the wording differs: al-Tabari and most others take it as one pelted with stars, Qatada as one cursed, and others as one reviled. On the exception, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi regard it as a sense of 'but' or as an exception from the protection, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir read it as an exception covering those who snatch a bit of news. On the nature of the flame, Ibn 'Abbas holds that it burns and disables without killing, whereas al-Hasan and a group say it kills; al-Qurtubi prefers the first view. The commentators, relying on the authentic hadith, describe how the devils used to climb to hear the angels and pass fragments to soothsayers with many lies added, and how their access was restricted at the birth of Jesus and then completely at the mission of the Prophet. Scholars differed on whether shooting stars existed before Islam, with most saying yes and others saying the protection became far stronger afterwards. Sayyid Qutb and Ibn 'Ashur present the verse as a sign of divine order and of the purity of revelation.

This verse explains that God guarded the heaven from accursed devils, who cannot approach it to learn what happens there. Only one who snatches a hasty hearing is pursued by a bright flame that burns him or leaves him deranged. The commentators agree on the general sense but differ on the nature of the shihab: Ibn 'Abbas holds that it wounds, burns and deranges without killing, while al-Hasan and a group say it kills, and al-Qurtubi finds the first view more sound. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate accounts of how the hearing is passed on: the devils climb upon one another, the highest seizes a word and hands it down until it reaches the soothsayers, who add many lies to it. Several authors report that the guarding of the sky intensified at the Prophet's coming, though al-Zuhri and Ibn Qutayba hold that the stoning existed earlier as well. Al-Razi and al-Alusi raise many rational objections to these reports and answer them, stressing God's absolute power. Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi limit themselves to the literal sense. Al-Sha'rawi distinguishes stealing from furtive eavesdropping, while modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb counsel keeping to the text without seeking further detail on the mechanics.

The commentators explain that God spread out the earth and set firm mountains upon it so that it would not sway with its people, and that He caused every kind of thing to grow in it in a determined and known measure. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and others agree that "mawzun" means what is fixed and known in a precise limit, citing Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ikrima and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi add that weighing here is a figure of speech for wisdom and balance: everything is set by a sound measure, with no excess or deficiency.

Others, such as al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Jawzi, take a literal sense and understand it as things that are actually weighed, such as gold, silver, copper, iron and kohl, and the minerals found in the mountains. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya nevertheless consider the first meaning broader and better.

On the "ma'ayish", al-Hasan and al-Baghawi understand food, drink and clothing, while al-Mawardi reads it as the means of earning a livelihood throughout life. For "those to whom you do not give provision", Mujahid and Ibn Kathir mention beasts and livestock, Mansur wild animals, and al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj slaves and servants; Ibn Kathir stresses that provision rests with God and not with people. Finally, Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi discuss the grammar: attaching "man" to the pronoun in "lakum" is allowed by some but criticised by the Basran grammarians.

In this verse God reminds people that He has made on earth the means of living for them, such as food, drink, clothing and ways of earning, and that He has also given them creatures whose provision does not fall on them. The commentators agree that the word maʿayish means the means of sustenance, and that the verse is a favour from God. They differ on who is meant by 'those for whom you are not providers'. Mujahid, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi say they are beasts and livestock, al-Tabari and Ibn Qutayba also mention wild animals, while al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj include slaves and maidservants along with the animals. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi take them to be dependants, servants and slaves whom people wrongly think they feed, since God is the true provider of all. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain the use of 'man', normally for rational beings, by the rule that when rational and non-rational beings are combined the rational ones predominate. On grammar, al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi allow 'man' to be linked to maʿayish or to the position of 'lakum', while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Atiyya note that linking it to the pronoun without repeating the preposition is weak in the view of the grammarians. Most commentators conclude that the central point is that God alone is the provider of everything people imagine they provide for, and God knows best.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that everything humans benefit from belongs to God, and that its sending down to creatures happens in a measure fixed by His wisdom and will, neither more nor less. Many, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, take the word "thing" here to mean mainly rain: according to Ibn Jurayj and al-Hasan it is distributed unevenly, and Ibn Mas'ud reports that no year is rainier than another, but God allots it where He wills. Others, such as al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari, hold that the term is broader and covers everything possible, with the treasuries serving as an image of divine power. Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi understand the treasuries as keys held in the heavens. On the fertilising winds, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada say they impregnate clouds and trees, while Abu Ubayda takes them to be winds that fertilise. As for the "earlier" and "later" generations mentioned next, Ibn Abbas identifies them as the dead and the living, Mujahid as earlier peoples and the community of Muhammad, and others as those who fell in battle or those in prayer rows. Taken together, the verse affirms God's knowledge, power and wisdom.

The commentators explain that this verse recounts a blessing of God: He sent fertilizing winds that load the clouds with water or pollinate the land and trees, then sent down rain from the sky to give drink to people, their animals and their lands. People do not hold the stores of this water, which belong to God alone. The exegetes agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that the winds fertilize the clouds so that they pour out rain, and they cite the report from Ibn Mas'ud; Ibn Kathir adds that the winds also pollinate the trees. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and those who follow them note that the word "lawaqih" may mean that the wind itself carries water, or that it fertilizes other things, or that it means "mulaqqihat" as Abu 'Ubayda held. Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i limit the fertilization to clouds or to trees depending on the transmission. Some report a hadith about the south wind, which Ibn Kathir judges weak, but no commentator settles between these readings. On the phrase "you are not its keepers", al-Tabari and Sufyan read it as "not preventers", while al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand that people cannot store the water in pools, springs and wells, and that God alone preserves it for their use. The passage continues with life, death, inheritance and God's knowledge of earlier and later generations.

This verse states that God alone gives life and causes death, and that He is the Inheritor who remains after all creatures have perished, inheriting the earth and all who dwell on it. The commentators agree that the verse demonstrates God's power and His sole authority over life and death, and recalls the resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the inheritance means God's survival after the annihilation of all beings, and al-Zamakhshari adds that the word is a metaphor borrowed from the heir of a deceased person. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur extend the giving of life to animals and plants alike, and Ibn Ashur sees in the verse an argument for the possibility of the resurrection.

The phrase about "those who go before and those who come after among you" is where opinions differ most. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Ikrima and most exegetes take it to mean the dead and the living, that is, all of humankind past and future; al-Tabari adopts this reading as the most sound given the context. Mujahid understands the earlier nations and the community of Muhammad, al-Hasan the obedient and the disobedient, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Jubayr the ranks in battle. Several scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir, also report that the verse was revealed concerning the ranks in prayer, when some men moved forward or back because of a beautiful woman praying behind the Prophet, though Ibn Kathir and others note the weakness of that report.

Most conclude that God will gather all people, for He is wise and all-knowing.

The commentators connect this verse to what precedes it, namely God's giving of life and death and His inheritance of the earth, and to what follows, the gathering on the Day of Resurrection. The broad meaning favoured by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy is that God knows all creatures completely: the 'foremost' (al-mustaqdimin) are those who have already died since Adam, and the 'latter' (al-musta'khirin) are those still living or yet to be born until the Day of Resurrection. He will gather them all, and this complete knowledge serves as proof of His power over resurrection.

The explanations of the terms vary. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and Muqatil take the foremost to be the dead and the latter to be the living, or past nations versus the community of Muhammad, or those already brought forth from men's loins versus those not yet. Al-Hasan understands those who hasten to obedience and those who lag behind, and Qatada those who rush to Islam and those who hold back. Al-Sha'bi reads them as the first and last of creation.

A widely circulated report, transmitted by Abu al-Jawza' from Ibn 'Abbas, says the verse was revealed about worshippers who jostled for the front rows or lagged behind to look at a beautiful woman praying behind the Prophet. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya regard this report as weak or strange, al-Tirmidhi considers Abu al-Jawza's version without Ibn 'Abbas more likely sound, and Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the surrounding verses weaken such narrow readings. Al-Qurtubi nonetheless calls it the most authentic of the reported causes of revelation.

This verse states that it is God who will gather all creatures for reckoning and recompense, and that He alone is able to do so. The commentators explain that it follows the statement that God gives life and causes death, and that He inherits the earth and those on it once they have passed away; the gathering is thus the natural continuation of this idea. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the meaning is God's complete knowledge of the first and last generations, and that gathering them after resurrection is easy for Him. As for "Wise, All-Knowing", several see in it proof that His wisdom requires recompense and that His knowledge encompasses every deed, as al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur note.

The scholars agree on the grammatical emphasis: the pronoun "He" affirms that the gathering belongs to God alone. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari connect the closing words to the idea that divine knowledge covers every state of creatures, whether their birth, their death or their conduct. Ibn 'Ashur also notes that calling God the Lord of the Prophet honours him, since his opponents denied the resurrection.

The commentators do not disagree on the core meaning. They differ mainly on how the verse connects with what precedes it: some see it as the conclusion of the proofs of divine power, others as a reminder of God's knowledge of past and future generations. None of them settles between these readings, which they present as complementary.

In this verse God says that He created Adam, the father of mankind, from salsal, dry clay that gives a ringing sound when struck, and from hama masnun, dark and altered mud. The commentators agree that "man" here refers to Adam, and that the verse recalls the origin of creation before mentioning the creation of the jinn from scorching fire. On the meaning of salsal, opinions differ. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba understand it as dry clay that rings, and al-Tabari judges this the most fitting reading since God elsewhere compares it to pottery. Mujahid and al-Kisai take it to mean foul-smelling mud, from the expression for meat that has rotted, while al-Farra takes it as clay mixed with sand and others as moist clay. As for masnun, several readings are given: altered and foul, the view of Mujahid, Qatada and Ma'mar; poured out, the view of Abu Ubayda; shaped into a form, as Sibawayh says; or smoothed. Some exegetes, such as Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, understand the verse as describing successive stages of the clay: dust, sticky clay, altered mud, and finally dry clay. Regarding the jinn, Ibn Abbas holds that the jinn's father is meant, al-Hasan and Qatada say Iblis, and the "scorching wind" is explained in various ways, such as a flame without smoke. Ibn Mas'ud, quoted by Ibn Kathir, describes it as one part of a fire seventy times hotter.

This verse states that God created man, namely Adam, from clay, sal-sal, a dry clay that rings when struck, drawn from black and altered mud. The jinn, it says, God had created earlier from the fire of samum. The commentators differ over who the jinn is: Ibn 'Abbas holds that he is the father of the jinn, just as Adam is the father of mankind, while Qatada, al-Hasan and others identify him with Iblis himself, created before Adam. They agree, however, on the meaning of samum, a scorching wind that penetrates the pores of the body and kills. Some describe it as a flame or a smokeless fire from which thunderbolts emerge, and others as the fire of hell. Ibn Mas'ud, transmitted by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, adds that this samum is only a seventieth part of the samum from which the jinn were created. The meaning of masnun is debated: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi stress a putrid or altered mud, while others such as Abu 'Ubayda and al-Baydawi take it to mean shaped or poured into a mould. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, that some jinn reproduce and eat and drink like humans while others do not, and that the devils, the offspring of Iblis, die only when he dies, whereas jinn may be believers or unbelievers. The verse thus underlines the greatness of God's creative power and prepares the account of the enmity between Adam and Iblis.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ what He said to the angels when He decided to create Adam: I am creating a human from dry clay, shaped from black and altered mud. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and others, 'when I have fashioned him' means giving him his form and completing his creation, and 'breathed into him of My spirit' means bringing him to life; God attributes the spirit to Himself as an honour, as az-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi point out. The prostration commanded is one of greeting and honour, not worship, which is the view the commentators generally share. Most agree that all the angels prostrated, but they differ on the force of 'all of them together': Sibawayh and al-Khalil take it as emphasis upon emphasis, while al-Mubarrad understands it as a simultaneous prostration. They also differ over Iblis: was he an angel, as Ibn 'Atiyya leans, or a jinn, as al-Hasan al-Basri reports? Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite a report from Ibn 'Abbas about angels burnt before Adam, which Ibn Kathir finds strange and likely Israelite, and so does not accept. Ar-Razi, finding it odd that God speaks directly to Iblis, answers that such speech is no honour when it is meant to humiliate. Az-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya read the verb 'to lead astray' as the cause being God's, with az-Zamakhshari explaining it as an incitement to the wrong path, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds that Iblis's offence was disobedience rather than disbelief, while others see in his argument a challenge to divine wisdom.

This verse says that once God has perfected Adam's form and breathed into him the spirit that makes him alive, the angels must prostrate before him. The commentators explain that perfecting means shaping the form and readying the body to receive the spirit, and that breathing is a figurative expression for conferring life, since no real breath was involved. Attributing the spirit to God is read as an honour given to Adam. Most, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, hold that the prostration was one of greeting and honour, not worship. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that some judged the angels superior to Adam, so that God tested them through this command, a view they attribute to the Mu'tazila. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that Iblis is named among the angels because he too was under the command, before being excepted. Scholars differ on Iblis's nature: some count him an angel, while al-Hasan, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi, held that he was of the jinn. Ibn Kathir considers the report from Ibn Abbas about angels burned by fire to be weak and probably Israelite in origin. On the meaning of salsal and hama masnun, views range from dry, ringing clay to foul-smelling or shaped mud. Several scholars, including Sibawayh and al-Khalil, read the phrase 'all of them together' as emphasis, while al-Mubarrad understood it as simultaneity.

This verse tells that after Adam was shaped and Allah breathed into him of His spirit, all the angels prostrated together in obedience to the command, with the exception of Iblis, who refused to be among those who prostrate. The commentators explain that the words 'all' and 'together' are there to rule out that some of them failed to prostrate or that they prostrated at different times. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh regard this as emphasis upon emphasis, while al-Mubarrad holds that 'together' shows they acted at one moment, a view Ibn al-Anbari adopted, though al-Zajjaj and most scholars rejected it because the word is definite and cannot function as a circumstantial clause. On whether Iblis was among the angels, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas and others, including al-Qurtubi, held that he was from the jinn and not an angel; al-Baydawi and others took the exception as disjunctive; al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya leaned toward his being an angel because he was addressed with the command. All agree that his refusal stemmed from arrogance and envy. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur explain that his argument from the origin of the material was a flawed judgment that led to his rejection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take 'rajim' to mean accursed and expelled. The prostration is generally understood as a greeting of honour, not an act of worship.

This verse reports that when God commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam, all of them did so except Iblis, who refused to be among those who prostrated. Al-Tabari explains the refusal as arrogance, envy and rebellion, and Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and al-Baghawi see it as pride and defiance: Iblis, created from fire, judged himself superior to Adam, who was made of clay, arguing that fire consumes clay. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi describe the refusal as disobedience joined with haughtiness, and some note that his answer implicitly questions God's wisdom. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi observe that the plain grammar of the exception would make Iblis one of the angels, whereas al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the exception is discontinuous because he was a jinn. Ash-Sha'rawi, relying on the verse in Surat al-Kahf, decides firmly that he was a jinn and not an angel, though he lived among them. On the prostration itself, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and at-Tha'labi state that it was an act of honour and reverence rather than worship. Most commentators agree that the refusal was a sin accompanied by pride, and that it led to Iblis being cast out of God's mercy.

God asks Iblis why he refuses to prostrate with the angels before Adam. Iblis replies that he will not prostrate before a human created from dry clay, black mud shaped into form, since he himself was created from fire, which he deems nobler. The commentators read the question as a rebuke that exposes the pride and envy that drove Iblis to disobey. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi agree that this proud answer lies at the heart of his disobedience. The word "rajim" is explained by Qatada and Ibn Juraij as cursed or driven away, and the curse is said to last until the Day of Judgment, which several take as meaning forever. On Iblis's nature, al-Hasan and Ibn Atiyya hold that he was a jinn and not an angel, while the majority, relying on the command addressed to the angels, count him among them; the former answer that angels may be called jinn because they are hidden. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that God addressed him directly, which is an honour if meant to exalt, but a humiliation if meant to abase. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the order to prostrate does not contradict the prohibition in Islam of prostrating to anyone other than God, since it was a gesture of respect and not an act of worship.

In this verse Iblis answers God's command to prostrate before Adam by refusing: it is not fitting, he says, that he should prostrate himself to a human created from dry clay, from black altered mud. Most commentators read this as a justification grounded in the superiority of origin, since Iblis was created from fire and Adam from earth, and fire consumes earth. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi see here the expression of his arrogance and envy, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take the lam in la-asjuda as emphasising the negation: it is not proper for him to prostrate. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this argument by analogy stands against the explicit text. Ibn Kathir, citing a report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas about the creation of the angels, calls it strange and of doubtful authenticity. On the word rajim, al-Tabari renders it as cursed, whereas Abu 'Ubayda and al-Shawkani connect it with being pelted by shooting stars. As for the expulsion, most place it either in Paradise or in the heavens, and several understand the curse until the Day of Judgement as lasting without end.

The commentators explain that God commands Iblis to leave his station among the angels, or the Garden according to some, and declares him rajim, meaning banished and stoned. They agree that the word means accursed and removed from God's mercy, and that the curse clings to him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that rajim means cursed or banished, and that in the Quran the root also carries the sense of reviling. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi read the verse as a warning that answers Iblis's argument, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that whoever opposes a text with analogy is himself accursed. They differ on the place of expulsion: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi mention the Garden, the heavens, or the company of angels, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi hold that he was removed from the rank of the exalted angels. On the phrase until the Day of Judgement, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and al-Razi take it as an open-ended duration or as lasting until he receives his punishment, while Ibn 'Ashur sees a curse that ends before a heavier retribution. Iblis then asks for respite until the Day of Resurrection; al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that he is granted a delay until the first blast of the trumpet, not as an honour but as an increase of his trial.

After commanding Iblis to leave Paradise, God declares that he is cast out and pelted, and that the curse will rest upon him until the Day of Judgment. The commentators agree on the general meaning: Iblis is banished from God's mercy and the curse follows him. Several of them, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, explain that mentioning the Day of Judgment is the furthest limit people use in speech, so it signifies endlessness. Ibn al-Jawzi adds that this day has no end, so it takes the place of eternity.

Al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi also note that this day may mark the point at which a punishment will be so severe that the curse is forgotten. This emphasises how harsh the coming punishment is. Al-Alusi reports another view: the curse from the creatures ends at the blowing of the trumpet, whereas God's curse continues without end.

Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that Iblis is cursed both in the heavens and on earth. Ibn Kathir adds, citing Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that Iblis's form changed after he was cursed. The commentators draw no legal rulings from this verse and confine themselves to explaining its meaning and purpose.

The verse records Iblis asking God for respite until the day they are raised, and God granting him a delay until the appointed time. Most commentators read Iblis's request as a wish not to die, or to gain time to mislead humanity. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the request was for survival and that God granted only a limited delay, not permanent life. Al-Mawardi reports from Ibn Abbas that the appointed time is the first blast of the trumpet, after which Iblis would die for forty years before the second blast. Others say that this time is known to God alone. Ibn Atiyya considers that the appointed time may be the Day of Judgment, without affirming it, and he sets aside weaker reports. Al-Razi lists several interpretations of the appointed time and does not settle among them.

Most exegetes agree that the respite was a trial, a means of separating the believer from God's enemy. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that divine wisdom kept Iblis as a test for mankind. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see the delay as a test for people and not as a favour to Iblis. Al-Zamakhshari notes that Iblis sought to prolong his life in order to harm humanity. Al-Razi examines at length whether misguidance may be attributed to God, reporting the answers of the various schools without deciding the matter himself.

This verse reports that God granted Iblis the respite he asked for, but only until the appointed time and not until the day of resurrection, so he will not die until all creatures have died. The commentators broadly agree that this appointed time is the first blast of the trumpet, when all creatures die, as Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report. They explain that the granting of his request was not an honour for Iblis but an increase in his trial and a test for mankind, as al-Samani, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi state. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that Iblis's request was to never die, since there is no death after the resurrection. Al-Mawardi also gives the view that the appointed time is known to God alone and unknown to Iblis, and reports Ibn 'Abbas's view that Iblis's death would last forty years, the interval between the two blasts. Scholars differ on how God addressed him: some say through a messenger, others say directly, but in the manner of a threat rather than an honour, as al-Qurtubi notes. Ibn Juzayy observes that Iblis's address of God as Lord shows he acknowledged lordship, yet this does not remove his disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur explains that his request arose from his corrupt nature. Al-Sha'rawi adds that Iblis believed he had escaped death, and that his arrogance was the cause of his downfall. Taken together, the verse presents this respite as a trial whose end remains known to God alone.

The commentators explain that after Iblis was expelled and cursed until the Day of Judgment, he asked God to delay his fate until the day of resurrection. God granted him a respite until the appointed time, not eternal life. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and the Jalalayn, identify this Appointed Time as the first blast of the trumpet, when all creatures die. They stress that this granting was no honour for Iblis but an increase in his trial and a test for humankind. Ibn Abbas and those who follow him say that Iblis would die for forty years, the interval between the two blasts. Others hold that the appointed time is known to God alone and hidden from Iblis. Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya report that Iblis wished not to die, and that this was refused. Al-Razi offers three possible meanings of the Appointed Time, the first blast, the term Iblis himself named, or a day known only to God, and discusses the theological difficulties that the passage raises. Ibn Ashur notes that the request reveals Iblis's malice and his desire to prolong his harm on earth.

The verse records Iblis's words to his Lord: because You led me astray, I will make sin appealing to people on earth and mislead them all, except Your sincere servants. The commentators broadly agree that "leading astray" means misguiding, and that "making appealing" means making disobedience and love of worldly things attractive. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the "sincere" are the believers who devoted their obedience and monotheism to God. Ibn Kathir adds that Iblis's followers will enter Hell, which has seven gates, each assigned a determined share of them. Al-Zamakhshari reads the particle "bi" as either an oath or a cause, and interprets the misguidance as God's command to Iblis to prostrate, which led to his own error; he holds that God is free of that error. Al-Sam'ani rejects this reading as contrary to Sunni belief, while al-Razi affirms that the attribution to God is literal and discusses the difficulties it raises. Reciters differ on the vowel of "al-mukhlisin": Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read with a kasra, meaning those who have made their devotion sincere, while the others read with a fatha, meaning those whom God has purified. On the phrase "this is a straight path leading to Me", some take it as a warning and others as a way that leads to God.

Iblis, addressing his Lord, declares that he will lead the children of Adam astray, but he makes an exception for God's sincere servants, those whom God has purified. The commentators agree that the mukhlasin are the believers who devoted their faith and worship to God alone. Al-Tabari reports from al-Dahhak that they are the believers, and al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn say the same, adding that they are those who made their obedience and monotheism pure. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy explain that sincerity means directing one's deeds to God without any worldly motive. Al-Mawardi illustrates this with the account that the disciples asked Jesus about the sincere person, and he answered that it is the one who acts for God and does not wish to be praised by people.

The readings also shape the meaning. The reading with a fatha on the lam makes God the agent: those You have chosen and purified, as Ibn Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. Al-Razi argues from this reading that sincerity itself comes from God's guidance and grace. The reading with a kasra on the lam, which Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi attribute to Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Abu Amr, describes those who devoted their deeds to God, and so puts the emphasis on the servant's own effort.

Al-Razi notes that Iblis made the exception so as not to be a liar, and that his scheme would have no effect on them. Ibn Ashur observes that the exception does not indicate how many sincere people there are compared with others. Al-Tabari reports that Qatada saw in the exception a favour from God himself. The commentators agree on the general sense but differ on the source of sincerity: whether it is a divine choice or an act the servant performs by his own will.

In this verse God answers Iblis: this is a straight path leading to Me, and Iblis will have no authority over My sincere servants, only over those who follow him among the misguided. The commentators offer several readings of the word 'alayya. Al-Hasan al-Basri takes it to mean "toward Me", so the path leads to God. Mujahid, followed by Qatada and Ibn Kathir, explains that the truth returns to God and that His way leads to Him. Al-Kisa'i, cited by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, reads it as a threat, like a man telling an opponent that his road passes by him and he will not escape, as in the verse "your Lord is ever watchful". Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as a binding obligation on God to uphold this way, meaning that He will not let Iblis dominate the sincere. Ibn al-Qayyim prefers the explanations of the early scholars and finds the threat reading ill-suited to the context.

The reading of Ya'qub, Ibn Sirin and Qatada, 'Aliyyun with a raised vowel, means elevated or lofty. Commentators also differ on what "this" refers to: some say the sincerity of the faithful, others the division of people into misguided and sincere. Several scholars, including Ibn 'Ashur, stress that only those already inclined to error fall under Satan's sway.

The exegetes also report that Hell has seven gates, each assigned to a particular group, according to the accounts of al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir.

This verse reports that God tells Iblis he has no power over His sincere servants, whom He has chosen and guided, and that his influence reaches only those among the misguided who choose to follow him. The commentators broadly agree on what 'authority' means: compulsion, dominion, or proof. Iblis cannot force anyone into error; he adorns and deceives, and the person then chooses. Al-Tabari and his peers read it mainly as the absence of any proof against the believers, whereas al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi understand it as force and dominance. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna explains that Iblis cannot drive the believers into a sin that God's pardon cannot cover.

The main disagreement concerns who the 'servants' are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take them to be the believers, the obedient or the purified, so the exception is disjunctive. Ibn al-Qayyim supports this reading and holds that the possessive expresses honour, while al-Zamakhshari treats the word as general and the exception as continuous. Al-Qurtubi draws from the verse the permissibility of excepting either a majority or a minority of a group, a point on which Ahmad ibn Hanbal and some grammarians disagree.

On recitation, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that some readers pronounced 'Aliyy, meaning 'exalted', while the majority reading 'Alayya is understood as 'towards Me'. In that reading the sentence carries a threat, according to al-Kisa'i and al-Zamakhshari. Regarding the seven gates of Hell, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report several enumerations, some traced to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, and linked to different groups of disbelievers.

The commentators explain that this verse continues God's words after Iblis declared his enmity and swore to lead the children of Adam astray. Hell is the promised destination of Iblis and of everyone among the misguided who followed him, all of them without exception. They agree that the pronoun in "their promised place" refers to the misguided or to the followers, and that "all of them" is an emphasis meaning totality. As for "it has seven gates", most take this to mean seven levels stacked one above another, each with a gate through which its people enter. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relay sayings of Ali describing this arrangement, and Ibn al-Jawzi transmits the names of the levels from Ibn Jurayj: Jahannam, Laza, al-Hutama, al-Sa'ir, Saqar, al-Jahim and al-Hawiya, a list also given by al-Baydawi. "A portion allotted" means a known share, which Qatada links to dwellings determined by deeds.

Opinions differ on who occupies each gate. Al-Dahhak assigns the first level to those who affirm God's oneness, who are punished according to their sins and then leave, followed by the Christians, the Jews, the Sabians, the Magians, the Arab polytheists and the hypocrites. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi report other classifications, some by categories of sin, and Ibn 'Atiyya holds that the gates may lie on one level within Hell itself. Several prophetic reports, such as those in al-Tirmidhi and cited by al-Qurtubi, are mentioned on this subject, but the commentators do not settle their authenticity.

This verse states that Hell is the meeting place of Satan and all who followed him, and that it has seven gates, each receiving a determined portion of the misguided. Most commentators understand the gates as levels stacked one above another. Al-Tabari transmits from 'Ali that the gates of Hell are layered, the first filling before the second, until all are full. Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Kathir and others list the seven levels as Jahannam, Laza, al-Hutama, al-Sa'ir, Saqar, al-Jahim and al-Hawiya. On who occupies each level, al-Dahhak says the first is for monotheists who will be punished according to their sins and then leave, followed by Christians, Jews, Sabians, Magians, Arab polytheists and finally hypocrites. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi repeat this order while noting other reports. Ibn 'Abbas, cited by al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud, assigns different levels to different groups, such as those who claim divinity, fire-worshippers and idolaters. Ibn 'Ashur sees the number seven either as a figure of multitude or as a reflection of the principal kinds of wrongdoing. Al-Razi explains the difference in shares by the unequal severity of disbelief. Al-Qurtubi also cites a report linking each gate to a category of sin, which he presents with reservations. The commentators do not settle between these readings.

This verse states that those who are mindful of God, meaning those who obey Him and avoid His prohibitions, will be in gardens and among springs. The commentators differ on the meaning of piety. Ibn Abbas and the majority of the Companions and Successors, as reported by al-Razi and al-Shawkani, understood it as guarding oneself from polytheism and disbelief, while al-Jubba'i and most Mu'tazilites took it to mean avoiding all sins, a view al-Razi found less convincing. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain the gardens as orchards and the springs as rivers, and al-Qurtubi adds that these are four rivers of water, wine, milk and honey. The following verses say they will enter in peace and safety, free from death, expulsion and affliction. All agree that the ghill is the hidden hatred and enmity in the heart, but they disagree on when God removes it. According to Abu Umama and several reports it happens after they enter Paradise, while al-Hasan places it in the Hereafter. Mujahid explains that they will be brothers on couches facing one another, so that no one sees the back of his companion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that Ali hoped he and Talha and al-Zubayr would be among them, which provoked an objection that no commentator resolves. Finally, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir connect the verse that follows, telling My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, to the need to combine hope and fear.

This verse states that the God-fearing, those who guarded themselves against associating partners with God and against sins, will be in gardens and springs, and it will be said to them: enter them in peace and security.
