The commentators agree that the sense is safety and security in Paradise, but differ on the word peace: al-Kalbi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take it as a greeting, from God or from the angels, while al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take it as simple soundness and safety. All agree that the hidden rancour in the heart, the ghill, is removed from the hearts of the people of Paradise, but they differ on when this happens: Abu Umama and several narrators place it after entry into Paradise, al-Hasan places it in the Hereafter, and Ibn Atiyya thinks it occurs at different stages. Al-Tabari reports that Ali applied the verse to companions, including those of the Battle of the Camel, a claim some rejected, while Ibn Kathir and others take it to refer to ten Companions. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari understand the removal as the purification of souls from envy and turbidity. According to Mujahid and others, the brothers on couches face one another so that no one sees another's back, and al-Zamakhshari adds that the couches turn with them. All agree that no weariness will touch them and that they will never be driven out, expressing an eternal bliss, which al-Razi reads as the absence of both spiritual and bodily harm.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the righteous in Paradise: they are told to enter in peace and safety, free from all fear and from any loss of their blessings, and God removes from their breasts the rancour and enmity that existed between them in this world, so that they become brothers, seated on couches facing one another, with no weariness and never to be expelled. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, agree that al-ghill is hidden hatred or enmity in the heart, and that facing one another means each sees the face of the other. Mujahid says no one looks at his companion's back, and al-Tabari adds that the couches turn with them wherever they turn. The scholars differ on when the removal happens. Abu Umama and most of the reports gathered by al-Tabari place it after entry into Paradise or at its gate, Ibn 'Atiyya thinks it occurs at several stages, while Ali ibn al-Husayn and al-Baydawi place it in this world, through the reconciliation of the Prophet's Companions. On who is meant, al-Tabari and others report that Ali hoped that he, Talha and al-Zubayr would be among them, and that some present objected; the commentators record the exchange without deciding between the parties. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari also discuss whether the 'pious' means those who avoid all sins or only polytheism. All agree that the bliss of Paradise is lasting and free of weariness.

This verse states that the God-fearing will feel no weariness in Paradise and will never be expelled from it, because their bliss is permanent. The commentators explain the word nasab as toil, exhaustion or hardship, and al-Shawkani and Ibn Sa'di note that the negation covers outward and inward fatigue alike. Al-Sam'ani, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir all describe it as the most explicit verse in the Quran on the eternity of the people of Paradise. Al-Razi reads it as a complete bliss that must be honoured, free from harm and lasting: the denial of fatigue answers physical harm, and the removal of rancour answers spiritual harm. On the meaning of piety the scholars differ. Al-Jubba'i and the Mu'tazila take the God-fearing to be those who avoid all sins, while Ibn 'Abbas, most Companions and Successors, as al-Razi reports, mean those who avoid polytheism and disbelief, a view al-Razi himself adopts. On the removal of rancour, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy report several views: it is the rancour of the pre-Islamic age according to 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, the rancour of worldly life according to al-Hasan, or a rancour that vanishes in Paradise according to the majority. Several works, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, transmit reports linking the verse to 'Ali and his companions, which others dispute, and the commentators do not judge between them. As for the next verse, Ibn 'Abbas says the promise of forgiveness applies to those who repent, and the occasion of revelation, transmitted by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, concerns companions who were laughing.

The verse tells the Prophet ﷺ to inform God's servants that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that His punishment is the painful punishment. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari and al-Baghawi, explains that forgiveness is for those who repent, while punishment is for those who do not. Al-Tabari sees in it both a warning against persisting in sin and a call to turn back in repentance. Many commentators, including al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Kathir, note that forgiveness and mercy are mentioned before punishment, which suggests that mercy prevails. Abu al-Su'ud draws from this that the "pious" addressed are not those who avoid every sin. Al-Zamakhshari presents the verse as a confirmation of what came before, and links it to the story of Abraham's guests so that people may take lesson from the fate of Lot's people. Al-Razi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi relate an occasion of revelation: the Prophet saw companions laughing and reminded them of Paradise and Hell, and Gabriel then brought this verse. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi point out the weakness of some of the chains for this report. Al-Qurtubi concludes that a person should warn and encourage himself, with fear dominating in health and hope in sickness. Ibn Sa'di adds that the heart should remain between fear and hope.

This verse states that God, speaking through His Prophet, is the Forgiving, the Merciful, toward those who repent and turn back to Him, and that His punishment is the painful punishment for those who persist in disobedience without repenting. It comes after the description of the reward of the pious and the torment of the wrongdoers, so that the contrast is clear. The commentators note that forgiveness and mercy are placed before punishment, which tilts the balance toward hope. Ibn 'Abbas explains that forgiveness is for the one who repents and punishment for the one who does not. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the verse combines hope and fear, and that the believer should hold both together. Qatada transmits a report, without a complete chain, that if a servant knew the extent of God's pardon he would not refrain from the forbidden, and if he knew the extent of His punishment he would destroy himself in grief. The most cited occasion of revelation, from Ibn Abi Rabah, is that the Prophet passed by companions who were laughing, and the verse was revealed to turn them away from despair. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a summary confirming what came before, and note that the mention of forgiveness shows the pious are not those who avoid every sin, small and great. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw the lesson that a believer should admonish himself and others with both fear and hope, moderation between them being the best course. The core meaning is agreed upon; the scholars differ on the order of the terms, the force of the emphasis, and the educational purpose of the passage.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the story of Abraham's guests, who were angels that greeted him and whom he feared because they did not eat. They announced to him a learned boy, who is Isaac according to the majority, and Abraham wondered at the good news given his old age and that of his wife. The angels replied that they had brought the truth and told him not to despair. The commentators agree that the word guest can be used for one or many, male or female, and that the visitors were angels. They differ on their number: Ibn Abbas mentions Gabriel with two others, Muqatil says twelve, and al-Suddi eleven. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain Abraham's fear by their refusal to eat, while al-Zamakhshari adds that they entered without permission. Mujahid reads Abraham's question as astonishment, whereas al-Zamakhshari takes it as a question about the manner of the good news. Muqatil reads 'alim as 'patient', while most read it as 'knowing'. The recitations differ on tubashshirun and yaqnut, both forms being recognized. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi link the story to the preceding verses, presenting it as a lesson that God forgives the repentant and punishes the wicked.

This verse describes the angels who entered upon Ibrahim as guests, greeted him, and his reply that he felt fear of them. The commentators explain that wajal means fear and inner unease. The most common explanation is that the guests did not eat the food he offered, so he became wary, since it was customary that a guest who does not eat is suspected of bad intentions. Al-Samani, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud give this reason. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi add that they had entered without permission and at an unusual time. Some report that he returned the greeting, though the verse does not say so explicitly, and several commentators draw on the accounts in Hud and al-Dhariyat.

The commentators agree that the word dayf applies to one or many, and that these guests were angels sent to bring Ibrahim the good news of a son and to destroy the people of Lot. Al-Tabari explains the word wajal as fear and notes that the plural verb agrees with the collective sense of dayf. Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi mention al-Hasan's reading lā tawjal with a different vowel on the taa, meaning do not be frightened.

The readings differ on nubashshiruka and tubashshirun, as al-Razi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note. The son announced is, according to the majority, Ishaq. Al-Mawardi reports the meaning 'knowing' for 'alim, while Muqatil reads it as 'forbearing'. Ibrahim wonders at the announcement given his old age, which all explain. The angels answer that the news is true and tell him not to despair of God's mercy, which, as al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir state, only the misguided do.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ about the guests of Abraham, the angels sent to give him the news of a son and to destroy the people of Lot. When they entered and greeted him, he felt fear, and they reassured him that they brought good news of a knowing boy, identified by the majority as Isaac. Abraham then wondered at the news, asking whether they gave him glad tidings when old age had already touched him. They answered that they brought the truth and that he should not be among those who despair. He replied that only those who go astray despair of their Lord's mercy. The commentators broadly agree that the word 'dayf' can refer to one or several guests, that 'wajal' means fear, and that the good news concerned a son. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain Abraham's astonishment by his age and that of his wife, while al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the question expresses surprise at news that goes against custom. Al-Mawardi reports two readings of the question: asking whether the news came from God to reassure him, or expressing wonder at what seemed unlikely. On the word 'alim', al-Mawardi cites the majority view that it means knowing, while Muqatil takes it to mean forbearing. On despair, all condemn it as a sin and note that Abraham did not actually fall into it; the warning is a general lesson. Variant readings such as 'tubashshirunni' or 'yaqnut' are accepted as legitimate forms of the same language.

The verse recounts the story of Abraham's guests, angels who came to give him the good news of a knowing boy, whom most commentators identify as Isaac, and who were also sent to destroy the people of Lot. When they gave the news, Abraham said in astonishment: do you give me good news when old age has already touched me? So with what do you give me good news? Most commentators read the question as an expression of wonder and surprise rather than doubt or denial. Mujahid says he marvelled at his own old age and that of his wife. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take 'ala' to mean 'along with', and the question as asking about the manner in which such a birth could come about under ordinary custom. The angels reply that they gave the news in truth, with certainty and no doubt. Abraham then rejects despair: who despairs of his Lord's mercy except those who have gone astray? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that Abraham was not in despair, but found the matter unlikely by the usual course of nature, and al-Zajjaj says much the same. Readers differ on the vowelling of the nun in 'tubashshirunni': Nafi reads it with a single kasra, Ibn Kathir with a doubled kasra, and the rest with fatha. The grammarians explain these readings, and none of them substantially changes the meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn link the passage to the verses that follow on God's mercy and punishment.

This verse reports that the angels who came to Abraham in the guise of guests gave him the glad tidings in truth, meaning with certainty, and told him not to be among those who despair. The commentators agree that the tidings concerned Isaac, and that Abraham marvelled at them because of his advanced age. The reply that only the misguided despair of God's mercy is cited by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, who regard despair of God's mercy as a grave sin. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that Abraham was not in despair but only found the event unlikely, a view Ibn Kathir also takes, since he hoped in God. Al-Razi argues that despair arises only from ignorance of God's power, knowledge and generosity. Al-Zamakhshari holds that Abraham's astonishment concerned the normal course of things rather than God's power, a view al-Alusi shares. The readers differ on the vowel of the verb yaqnat and on whether the word qanitin is read with or without an alif; al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya treat both readings as valid, and al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that both verb forms exist in Arabic with the same meaning. Al-Razi adds that a prohibition addressed to a prophet does not imply he had committed the act.

This passage recounts Abraham's reply when the angels gave him the good news of a knowing boy. Astonished that a son should come to him in old age, he was told they had brought him a true and certain tidings, and he did not despair. As the commentators explain it, Abraham denies that he is one of the despairing, and says that only those who go astray despair of God's mercy, meaning those who are ignorant of the vastness of His mercy, knowledge and power. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir largely agree that the question is a rhetorical denial and that Abraham was not in despair; he only found the news hard to believe according to ordinary custom, not with regard to God's power. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Suyuti report that despair of God's mercy is among the grave sins, as is feeling secure from His plan, and al-Baghawi cites a tradition and al-Tahawi's remarks on balancing fear and hope. On recitation, the readers differ on the vowel of yaqnutu: Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read with a kasra, the others with a fatha, and al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi consider both forms valid; Abu 'Ubayda rejected the kasra, a view Ibn 'Atiyya answers. As for al-dallun, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan take it as those who stray from the right way or the disbelievers, while Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi render it as unbelievers or losers.

The verse records Abraham's question to the angels who came to him in the guise of guests: what is your business, and what grave mission brings you after the good tidings? They replied that they were sent against a criminal people, the people of Lot, idolaters steeped in wrongdoing, to destroy them. They excepted the family of Lot, meaning his followers and those of his faith, who would be saved, and then his wife, who would be among those left behind. The commentators agree on the broad meaning: being sent means punishment and destruction, the family of Lot means the believers who followed him, and his wife, who remained an unbeliever, joined the criminals. Many dwelt at length on grammar. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Attiyya hold that the first exception is disconnected if it refers to the people, and connected if it refers to the pronoun of the criminals; Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also discuss whether the second exception is an exception from an exception, which Zamakhshari rejects in this case. On the verb qaddarna, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Abbas read it as we decreed, Ali ibn Isa as we wrote, and al-Zajjaj as we arranged. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take it as the angels speaking like the close attendants of a king who claim his orders for themselves, while others take it as God's own words not reported from the angels. The ghabirin are those who remain in the punishment. Abraham asked because he knew angels descend only for a grave matter, and an announcement of a son alone would not require so many messengers.

The angels tell Abraham that they have been sent to a people of criminals, meaning the people of Lot, who had persisted in disbelief and wrongdoing. The commentators agree that the "family of Lot" refers to his believing followers, whom God would spare. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that this exception is disconnected, since those believers were not criminals, while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi read it as connected to the word "criminals", meaning that these believers did not commit the crime. All agree that Lot's wife, who was an unbeliever, was not saved and was counted among those destined for destruction. Scholars differ on the meaning of "qaddarna": al-Nakha'i and al-Qurtubi take it to mean "we decreed", Ali ibn Isa "we wrote", and al-Zajjaj "we arranged". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the angels attribute the decree to themselves because of their closeness to God, as the close servants of a king say "we have decided". Mujahid reports that Lot did not recognise his visitors, and that the "torment" they mention is the punishment of Lot's people. The readers vary in how certain words are pronounced, but all agree on the main point: destruction falls on the criminals and salvation on the believers.

The commentators explain that when Abraham asked the angels about their mission, they replied that they had been sent to destroy the people of Lot, described as criminals, meaning polytheists steeped in wrongdoing, except the family of Lot, his followers and those who shared his faith, all of whom would be saved. As for his wife, God has decreed that she would remain among those left to the punishment, because of her disbelief. The scholars discuss the grammar of the exception. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that it is disconnected if it refers to the people, since they are defined by their crime and the family of Lot were not criminals, but connected if it refers to the pronoun in 'criminals'. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur consider it disconnected. Al-Zamakhshari treats the exception concerning Lot's wife as attached to the pronoun in 'we will save them', while Abu Hayyan accepts that it may be an exception from an exception. Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn al-Jawzi note that she ultimately returns to the criminal people. All agree on the meaning of 'qadarna' as we decreed or determined, and of 'al-ghabirin' as those who remain. Attributing the decree to the angels, though it belongs to God, is explained as a sign of their closeness to Him, like the courtiers of a king. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'lamunjuhum' with a light form of the verb, while the others use the intensive form.

The verse tells us that when Abraham asked the angels about their mission, they replied that they had been sent to destroy the people of Lot, who were criminals, meaning idolaters persisting in sin. They excepted the family of Lot, that is his household and the believers who followed him, whom they promised to save. Then they excepted his wife: God decreed that she was among those who would remain in the punishment, because she was an unbeliever like the others. The word 'ghabirin' is understood by most as those who remain behind, though some take it as those who perish or pass away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that she stayed with the people until their destruction. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and al-Razi point out that the exception can be read in two ways: if the first is disconnected and the second connected, the wife falls under the doomed. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, adopts this reading, while Ibn 'Atiyya discusses its grammar and cites al-Mubarrad. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also note that the angels ascribe the decree to themselves out of closeness to God, as the courtiers of a king speak of what they have decided. On the meaning of 'qaddarna', some take it as 'we decided', others as 'we wrote' or 'we ordained'. The recitation variants of 'lamunajjuhum' and 'qaddarna', with or without shadda, are reported together with their grounds.

When the messengers came to Lot's family, Lot said he did not know them. They answered that they had come to bring the punishment his people had doubted, with certain truth, and that they were truthful in what they announced. Al-Tabari and Mujahid explain that the word munkarun means that he did not recognise them, while many commentators see in it the strangeness of these guests. Al-Zamakhshari reports that Lot feared they might bring him harm, and that the messengers' reply removes this fear by telling him of the ruin of his enemies. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi repeat the description of these visitors as handsome young men, and Ibn Kathir notes that the announcement concerns the end of the people. Then, according to al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, the angels order Lot to leave by night with his household, to follow behind them, and that none of them should look back, while the destruction is to come at morning. Regarding the destination, Ibn 'Abbas says Syria, Muqatil names Zughar, and others mention Egypt or the land of Abraham. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi explain the prohibition on looking back as a way to keep the heart from clinging to those left behind or to avoid the sight of the punishment.

This verse records Lot's words to the messengers who came to his house: you are a people I do not know. The commentators agree that he did not recognise them, as Mujahid reports and al-Tabari explains, meaning that he did not know them. The messengers replied that they had come to him with what his people had been doubting, namely the punishment, and that they spoke the truth. Al-Zamakhshari explains that Lot felt aversion and feared they would bring him some evil, a reading also followed by al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi. Al-Razi gives three possible reasons for his words: he did not know them, they were handsome young men whom his people might harm, or he did not know their origin or purpose. Al-Qurtubi also stresses his fear for their good looks. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur note that the reply of the messengers aims to remove this anxiety by announcing good news to Lot. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, connect the passage to the story of Abraham and the good news of a son. The explanations therefore differ on why Lot doubted them, and no commentary decides between them.

The commentators explain that when the angels came to Lot in the form of handsome young men, he did not recognise them and said he did not know them. They replied that they had not come with what he feared, but with the punishment his people doubted and denied, and that they had brought the certain truth and spoke the truth. Most agree that the word yamtarun means that the people doubted and disputed the threat, since Lot warned them of punishment and they did not believe him, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud report. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take bal as a correction of Lot's fear of a hostile visit: the angels brought what would delight him, namely the punishment of his enemies. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the preposition in bil-haqq may express accompaniment, meaning the angels came bearing the truth. Al-Qurtubi and al-Tha'alibi report that Lot did not know them, or feared for them because of the desire of his people aroused by their beauty. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi say the punishment is the destruction of Lot's people, and that the double emphasis of the angels was meant to reassure him.

The commentators explain that the angels, who had come to Lot and whom he did not recognise, answer him that they bring the punishment his people had doubted, and that they bring him the certain truth and are sincere in what they report. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take this truth to be the punishment that struck Lot's people, and the oath of sincerity as a confirmation of what they had announced: the destruction of the wrongdoers and the deliverance of Lot. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the words "Nay, rather" dismiss Lot's fear that the visitors brought him harm, since they bring what should gladden him, namely the punishment he had threatened his people with. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand the truth as a certainty leaving no room for doubt. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that the emphasis of the particle "inna" shows Lot's eagerness to believe them. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that repeating the verb in the form "to come" is a stylistic variation rather than a repetition. The scholars do not settle the finer points: some stress the announcement of the punishment, others its reality, yet all agree on the general sense of the verse, which is an assurance given to Lot.

This verse records the angels' command to Lot to set out at night with his family, after part of the night has passed, to walk behind them so as to guard and watch over them, to let no one look back, and then to head to the place they are told to go. The commentators broadly agree that the departure was before dawn, with Lot at the rear, and that the prohibition on looking back means not dwelling on what is happening to the people behind or being distracted by it. On the phrase "a portion of the night", Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi say it refers to its last part, Muqatil says a part of it, and Qutrub says its darkness, a view cited by al-Mawardi.

Al-Tabari, quoting Mujahid, explains that no one should look behind, and Qatada reports that Lot was commanded to be behind his household, following the last of them. Ibn Kathir sees in this a role of guardianship, like the Prophet's conduct on campaign, shepherding the weak. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say Lot was at the rear to watch over his people and hasten them, while al-Razi lists several reasons for the prohibition: that no one should be left behind and struck, that no one should see the great calamity, that they should hurry, and that no one should keep attachment to what he left. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also note that the prohibition may serve as an image of continuing the journey without pause.

Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, identify the destination as al-Sham, the Levant, while others suggest Egypt, the Jordan region, or an unspecified place of safety.

This verse tells us that Allah revealed to Lot His decree: the people will be completely uprooted, first and last, when they enter the morning. The commentators explain that "dabir" means the last of them, or according to some the root, so the phrase denotes total annihilation with no survivor. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas and Qatada, and Ibn Kathir keep to the plain sense that the destruction will come at dawn. They also report that the men of the city, that is Sodom, rejoiced at the arrival of the guests, intending to commit the abomination. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain the command not to look back as meant to hasten the journey, to spare the travellers from dwelling on the fate of the wrongdoers, and to keep the group together. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also see in the vague phrase "that affair" followed by its explanation a way of stressing its gravity. On recitation, al-A'mash's reading with the kasra on "inna" is noted by Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan as a variant that is not part of the Quranic text. As for the destination, Ibn Abbas identifies it as al-Sham, while others mention Egypt or a village among the towns of Lot's people. The commentators report these views without deciding between them.

The verse describes the people of the city of Lot, Sodom, coming to his house joyful and eager upon hearing that guests had arrived, intending to commit lewdness with them. Commentators explain that their rejoicing was the anticipation of this act. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that some of them gave each other the good news. Several, including al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi, state that the guests were angels, though Lot did not yet know this, as Ibn Kathir notes. Ibn Atiyya judges it more likely that this visit came before Lot learned of the coming destruction, while acknowledging that the conjunction wa does not require strict order and that the visit could have followed his knowledge. The people had a habit of molesting strangers, which is why they reminded Lot of his earlier prohibition on hosting anyone. On the offer of Lot's daughters, opinions differ: Qatada and others take them as his own daughters, while al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir understand the women of his people, since a prophet is a father to his community. The oath "By your life" is taken by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi as a divine oath honouring the Prophet Muhammad, whereas al-Zamakhshari attributes it to the angels speaking to Lot. Commentators explain sakra as delusion or heedlessness and ya'mahun as wavering or bewilderment.

This verse records Lot's words to his people when the men of Sodom came to him rejoicing at his guests, whose faces they had found beautiful, hoping to commit indecency with them. He said: these are my guests, do not disgrace me concerning them, fear God and do not humiliate me. The commentators agree that honouring the guest is a duty and that wronging a guest is wronging the host, so disgrace here means the shame that falls on the host. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'labi report that the people answered by reminding him that he had forbidden them to host or shelter any outsider, while al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi give another reading of that prohibition, namely that he had forbidden them to let strangers enter the city. On the phrase my daughters, opinions differ: Qatada and most who cite him take it to mean his own daughters, whom he offered in marriage; others take it to mean the women of his people, since a prophet is like a father to his community. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the first reading would imply that a believing woman may marry an unbeliever under his law, and he treats the phrase as a rhetorical exaggeration meant to shame them. Az-Zamakhshari attributes the oath la'amruka to the angels speaking to Lot, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and most commentators understand it as an oath by the life of the Prophet Muhammad, an honour. All agree the people are described as lost in their intoxication and confusion, which leads to the cry and the stones of baked clay that followed.

The verse recounts that when Lot's people came rejoicing at his guests, seeking to commit a shameful act, Lot told them these were his guests and not to disgrace him, and to fear God and not humiliate him. Most commentators understand khizy as humiliation and disgrace, while some, such as Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, allow the sense of shame and embarrassment. All agree that Lot reminds them of the duty owed to a guest and the protection owed to a neighbour, and al-Zamakhshari notes that whoever wrongs a guest wrongs his host. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir hold that this exchange took place before Lot knew his visitors were messengers of God. The exegetes also report that the people had earlier forbidden him to host strangers, which explains their reply: did we not forbid you from hosting anyone? Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, following Qatada, take his words about my daughters as an offer of marriage, while others read them as referring to the women of his people, since a prophet is a father to his community, and Ibn 'Atiyya sees a rhetorical device with no real permission intended. Finally, the oath la'amruka, by your life, is reported by Ibn 'Abbas and most commentators as addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, an honour unique to him, whereas al-Zamakhshari attributes it to the angels speaking to Lot, a view Ibn al-Qayyim rejects in defending the traditional reading.

This verse belongs to the story of Lot, when his people came rejoicing at the news of his guests, hoping to commit an abomination with them. Lot replied that these were his guests, begged them not to shame him and to fear God. They answered with a rhetorical question of rebuke: Had we not forbidden you from hosting people from among the worlds? On the plain sense, the commentators largely agree that this means forbidding him to host or shelter strangers. Al-Tabari and Qatada take it as a prohibition on hosting anyone, while al-Zamakhshari explains that these people attacked every stranger, Lot did his utmost to stop them, and they threatened to expel him. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi offer an alternative reading: they forbade him to let outsiders enter the town. As for Lot's words, 'these are my daughters', interpreters differ: Qatada held that he meant his own daughters, while others took it to mean the women of his people, since a prophet is like a father to his community. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that the first reading would imply that a disbeliever may marry a believing woman under that law, which he considers unlikely. The phrase 'By your life' (la-'amruka) is, for most commentators such as Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, an oath by God on the life of the Prophet Muhammad, an honour which Ibn 'Abbas said God granted to no one else. Al-Zamakhshari, however, attributes it to the angels speaking to Lot, and the wording does not clearly settle the matter.

This passage reports Lot's words to his people when they come seeking his guests: "These are my daughters, if you must act." The commentators understand him to direct them to what is lawful, marriage with women, and to forbid the grave sin of relations with men. All agree on this general meaning. They differ on the word "my daughters." Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and, in one of his suggestions, Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean his own daughters, while al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that he meant the women of the people, since a prophet is like a father to his community. Ibn 'Atiyya also notes that Lot may have spoken hyperbolically and reproachfully, like someone telling a man about to kill another: "Kill me instead." Al-Zamakhshari attributes the words of verse 72 to the angels, whereas the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi, read the oath "by your life" as addressed to the Prophet, God swearing by his life as an honour; Ibn 'Abbas said God never swore by anyone else's life. "Sakra" is understood as heedlessness or error, and "ya'mahun" as bewildered wandering, though Qatada reads it as playing. Al-Tabari reports that the verse refers to the Quraysh, an opinion Ibn 'Atiyya considers remote from the context. The commentaries add that the cry seized them at sunrise, that the city was overturned, and that the "mutawassimin" are attentive observers, perceptive people, or those who reflect.

In this verse God swears by the life of the Prophet ﷺ, an honour that the commentators stress strongly, and states that those people are lost in their drunken error, wandering in confusion. Ibn 'Abbas explains la-'amruka as meaning by your life or your existence, and says God never swore by the life of anyone else. Qatada reads sakra as error and ya'mahun as playing, al-A'mash reads sakra as heedlessness, and Mujahid reads ya'mahun as hesitating. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the address is to the Prophet and that the people meant are the Quraysh, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan take the pronoun to refer to the people of Lot. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi also report that the oath may have been spoken by the angels to Lot. The scholars agree on the nobility of this oath and on the form 'amr, the lighter vowelling reserved for oaths because they are so frequent. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i disliked saying la-'amri when swearing by one's own life, while Ibn Habib advised keeping the phrase for this verse. For all of them, the sudden punishment at sunrise is the consequence of their error.

The verse describes the punishment that struck the people of Lot: a cry seized them at sunrise. According to al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, the torment began at dawn and was completed at sunrise. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya, understand this cry as a terrible punishment, while al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud identify it as the cry of Gabriel. Al-Razi notes that the verse does not establish this identification without strong evidence. On the oath 'By your life', most, with Ibn 'Abbas, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani, take it as God's oath honouring the Prophet, peace be upon him, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that it may be spoken by the angels to Lot. The word 'sukra' is explained as delusion and heedlessness, and 'ya'mahun' as wandering in confusion. Al-Tabari applies the passage to the Quraysh, a view Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider remote from the context. The 'mutawassimin' are, for Mujahid, those who discern, for Qatada those who take warning, and for others those who reflect. The 'enduring path' refers to a clear road that travellers to Syria pass, which serves as a warning to the Quraysh. The overall meaning is a lesson for those who reflect on the severity of this punishment.

This verse reports that God overturned the towns of Lot's people, making their highest part the lowest, and rained down on them stones of sijjil, understood as clay hardened or baked. The commentators agree on the general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd explain the word mutawassimin as those who discern closely, reflect and take lessons, while Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean those who look attentively. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a hadith on the insight of the believer who sees by the light of God, though they note that its chains of transmission are weak. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi list these meanings and consider them close to one another.

Opinions differ on the stones and the cry. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi report that sijjil means clay, and that some understand it as clay bearing a written mark, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Asma'i suggest the word may not be Arabic. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi describe the cry as a shattering blast, which some attribute to Gabriel, occurring at sunrise according to al-Qurtubi. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that the ruins remain visible on the road to Syria used by the Quraysh, a warning to them. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain the road as clear, while Ibn 'Abbas describes it as a lasting ruin.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the account of the destruction of Lot's people. It states that what befell them, the overturning of the city and the rain of baked clay stones, contains signs and lessons for those who look carefully and reflect. Most agree on the meaning of 'al-mutawassimin': those who look closely, who read signs, who reflect or take warning, these senses being close to one another. Mujahid says they are the discerning (al-mutafarrisin), Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak say observers, Qatada those who take warning, and Muqatil and Ibn Zayd those who reflect. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi explain that the root means a mark by which one knows something. Many cite the hadith 'Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of God', which the Prophet is said to have recited after this verse, though al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani note that its chain is weak or singular.

They differ on the nature of this insight. Al-Hasan and some scholars of meaning take it as inference from evident signs, such as the reasoning that the One who destroyed Lot's people can destroy the disbelievers. Others, including Ibn al-Qayyim, take it as a light God casts into the heart, and he distinguishes several kinds of insight: faith-based, ascetic and physiognomic. Al-Qurtubi reports that the Sufis regard it as a miraculous gift, while others regard it as reasoning from signs. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as an indirect address to the Quraysh, who had not been deterred by these examples.

Most agree that 'that' refers to the whole story, and that 'it is on a lasting road' refers to the ruins still visible along the route the Quraysh used to travel to Syria, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri indicate.

The commentators explain that the phrase "and it lies on a lasting road" means that the towns of Lot's people, that is Sodom and its surroundings, remain visible on a clear, enduring route that travellers pass and whose traces they can see. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take "muqim" to mean a clear, marked road, while Ibn Abbas understands it as an everlasting destruction. Most read the pronoun "it" as referring to the destroyed city or towns, though some link it to the signs, the stones or the cry. The exegetes agree that this route is the one the Quraysh used on their journeys to Syria, and that they pass these ruins, so the verse serves as a warning and a lesson to them, as in the verse of the Saffat: "You pass by them in the morning and at night." Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan connect the verse to the preceding statement about signs for the discerning, so the lesson is open to any attentive observer. On the meaning of "that", nearly all agree that it refers to the cry, the overturning of the city and the rain of baked clay stones. The believers are those who draw the lesson from it, recognising that this punishment followed from disobedience and disbelief. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the verse affirms God's vengeance against the corrupt and the lasting trace of that punishment for those who reflect. The shared view is therefore the endurance of the ruins and the value they hold as an example.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the account of the destruction of Lot's people at Sodom, with the cry of punishment, the overturning of the city and the rain of baked clay stones. Its plain meaning is that in this destruction there is a clear sign and proof for those who believe in God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr illustrated it with a man who sends his signet ring to his family so they will recognise that his message is true. All agree the punishment was evident, and that "for the believers" means those who benefit from it. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that the verse also addresses the Quraysh, who pass the ruins on their trade route to Syria, a road that is still visible and has not disappeared. Abu al-Su'ud notes that the singular "ayah" follows the earlier plural because what is now visible is the remaining traces rather than the whole story. The main differences concern the pronoun in the preceding verse, which some refer to the cities, others to the stones or the cry, though this does not change the meaning of this verse. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also cite the hadith on the insight of the believer, transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, which commentators link to the word "mutawassimin". The general message is therefore one of lesson and careful observation.

God states that the people of al-Ayka, meaning the people of Shu'ayb, were wrongdoers, that is, disbelievers who had transgressed the limits. The commentators explain that al-Ayka is a thicket or a dense cluster of trees, and most of their trees were doum palms. Nearly all agree on the punishment: God sent a scorching heat upon them for seven days, then a cloud came, under whose shade they sought refuge, and it rained fire upon them until they were destroyed. On the pronoun in 'and they are', opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur take it to refer to the two towns, the town of the people of Lot and the town of the people of al-Ayka, which lie on a clear road that travellers, including the Quraysh on their journeys to Syria, pass by. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi allow that it may refer to al-Ayka and Madyan, since Shu'ayb was sent to both. As for the word imam, the commentators agree that it means the path that is followed and taken as a guide, al-Tabari and Mujahid describing it as a clearly marked road, while al-Sudda takes it to mean a manifest book. They also agree that the account is meant to prompt reflection and to serve as a lesson.

God states that He punished the People of the Thicket, the people of Shu'ayb, who lived among dense thick trees, because of their wrongdoing, which the commentators describe as polytheism, highway robbery and cheating in measure and weight. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, He first sent a scorching heat that lasted seven days, then a cloud from which fire rained down and consumed them. Most commentators, including al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Jalalayn, understand the pronoun in 'and they are' as referring to the towns of the people of Lot and of the People of the Thicket, and the phrase 'a clear path' as a road that travellers pass along and can learn from. Ibn Juzayy, al-Razi and al-Baydawi add that the pronoun may instead refer to the Thicket and Madyan, since Shu'ayb was sent to both, or to Lot and Shu'ayb themselves. Al-Suddi reads 'imam' as a clear book, while the majority, following Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, take it to mean a road, a sense that al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain by the fact that a road is followed by those who travel it. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani note that the Thicket is a region between the Hijaz and Syria, on the route used by the Quraysh caravans, which is why the verse is taken as a warning to them. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur add that the pronoun may designate two tribes of the Thicket and Madyan.

This verse speaks of the People of al-Hijr, that is the people of Thamud who lived in the valley known as al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and the Levant. They denied the messengers, and most commentators take this to mean their prophet Salih alone. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and others explain that whoever denies one messenger has in effect denied all of them, since they share the same monotheism and fundamental principles that do not vary across nations or ages. Al-Zamakhshari also mentions the view that the plural includes Salih and the believers with him. The commentators report that God gave them signs, above all the she-camel brought forth from a hard rock at Salih's call, with her miraculous birth, great size and abundant milk, yet they turned away from her. They carved homes into the mountains, feeling secure from collapse, enemies and misfortune, but a blast seized them at morning on the fourth day, and their wealth and fortresses availed them nothing. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi cite the hadith in which the Prophet, passing through al-Hijr during the expedition to Tabuk, forbade his companions to enter their dwellings unless weeping, lest they suffer the same fate, and hurried on. On the meaning of al-Hijr, Qatada and al-Zajjaj say it is the name of the valley, al-Zuhri and Muqatil that it is the name of the town, and al-Tabari a land between the Hijaz and Syria. Some, such as al-Alusi, connect the passage to consoling the Prophet over his people's rejection.

This verse tells that the people of Thamud, who dwelt in al-Hijr between the Hijaz and al-Sham, denied their prophet Salih. God had given them signs confirming the truth of his message, chief among them the she-camel brought forth from the rock, yet they turned away from them and took no lesson. The commentators list several signs in the camel: her emergence from the rock, her swift calving, her great size, and the abundance of her milk, which sufficed for all of them. They agree that denying one messenger amounts to denying all, which is why the plural is used although only Salih was rejected; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state this, and al-Zamakhshari adds that it may mean Salih together with the believers who followed him. They differ on the meaning of al-Hijr: al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi cite that it is the name of a valley, while al-Zuhri and Muqatil take it as the name of their city, and al-Tabari describes a region between the Hijaz and al-Sham. On the phrase about dwellings hewn from the mountains in safety, al-Mawardi records four readings: safe from the mountain falling on them, from ruin, from punishment, or from death. Ibn Atiyya judges the most sound view to be that they felt secure against the consequences of the hereafter and so did not act accordingly. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that a cry seized them at dawn on the fourth day, and that their wealth did not avail them.

This verse describes the people of al-Hijr, the Thamud, the people of Salih, who carved their homes out of the mountains and felt safe in them. The commentators differ on the meaning of being secure. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand it as safety from collapse, from thieves breaking in and from enemies, since their houses were strongly built. Al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan take it as safety from God's punishment or from death, the Thamud thinking the mountains would protect them. Ibn 'Atiyya considers it most apparent that they felt secure against the consequences of the Hereafter and acted according to that sense of safety alone, a view Ibn Kathir follows, adding that they carved their homes out of pride and needless excess. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi record several parallel opinions. All agree on the outcome: the cry seized them in the morning, and their wealth did not save them. Al-Tabari places the cry on the fourth day after they slaughtered the she-camel, which Ibn Kathir also relates to the same episode. Most commentators hold that rejecting one prophet amounts to rejecting all of them, as Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy explain, while al-Zamakhshari also allows that the plural may refer to Salih and his believers. For al-Shawkani and al-Qasimi, the lesson is that material power brings no help when God's decree arrives. Sayyid Qutb sees in the verse the picture of a false sense of security that precedes ruin.

This verse describes the destruction of the people of Thamud, the dwellers of al-Hijr, who denied their prophet Salih and slaughtered the she-camel that was a sign from God. The Cry seized them as they entered the morning, and neither their houses hewn from the mountains nor their wealth and strength availed them. The commentators agree that the Cry was a destroying punishment. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that God first afflicted them with scorching heat for seven days, and Ibn Kathir adds that their houses were built out of pride and wantonness rather than need. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the most apparent meaning of their feeling of safety to be that they felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter and therefore did not act accordingly, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and others mention security from collapse, theft or death. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi describe the Cry as the cry of punishment, Abu Hayyan reports that it may have been the voice of Gabriel, and al-Alusi explains that it led to the earthquake mentioned in surah al-A'raf. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi note that some reports place the Cry after mid-morning, and suggest reading the word morning as an extended period of time. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as one of a series of stories of peoples struck in similar ways.

This verse states that the wealth and the homes carved into the mountains by the people of Thamud did not benefit them when the punishment seized them at dawn through the Cry. The commentators agree that what they had acquired could not save them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti take this to mean their sturdy buildings, wealth and numbers. Ibn al-Jawzi offers two readings, either the carving of the mountains or their goods and livestock. Ibn Kathir identifies the crops and fruit whose water they withheld from the she-camel, to the point of slaughtering her. Ibn 'Atiyya rejects the reading about the safety of their houses and suggests instead that these people felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter and acted accordingly. Abu al-Su'ud notes a note of mockery in the phrasing, and that the particle fa marks the failure of their wealth at the exact moment of punishment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy recount the story of the people of Salih, while Ibn Sa'di stresses that rejecting one messenger amounts to rejecting all. Modern commentators such as al-Sha'rawi and Sayyid Qutb draw the lesson that no shelter can avert God's decree.

This verse states that God did not create the heavens, the earth and what lies between them in vain, but "with truth", meaning with justice and for the recompense of deeds, rewarding the doer of good and punishing the wrongdoer. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand "truth" as justice, and say God did not wrongly destroy the peoples mentioned in the surah. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain it as creation grounded in wisdom and benefit, so that lasting corruption does not suit the order of the world, which justifies removing the corrupters. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as the arrangement of things in accordance with wisdom, whose truth eventually becomes manifest.

The verse then affirms that the Hour will certainly come and that God will avenge His Messenger on his enemies there. It commands him to pardon with a beautiful pardon, that is, to turn away from the disbelievers without resentment. Ali and Ibn 'Abbas say this means being content without reproach, and al-Mawardi reports several meanings, including turning away without distress and forgiving without rebuke.

The main disagreement concerns abrogation. Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and others hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, and that this forbearance preceded the command to fight. Al-Hasan takes it as concerning the Prophet's personal conduct and not abrogated, and al-Alusi and al-Tayyibi similarly hold that it enjoins good conduct and patience. Al-Razi finds abrogation unlikely, since the aim is to show nobility of character.

The verse ends by describing God as the Creator and the All-Knowing, who is aware of people and their deeds, which consoles the Prophet and affirms the resurrection.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the account of the destruction of peoples who rejected their messengers. It affirms that God created the heavens, the earth and what lies between them only with truth, that is, with justice, that the Hour is certainly coming, and that the Prophet should forgive his people with a beautiful forgiveness. The verse ends by saying that your Lord is the Creator, the All-Knowing, who knows people and their deeds.

The scholars largely agree that "truth" here means justice and wisdom. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as justice, so creation is not in vain and recompense is given with fairness. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi understand it as the wisdom that requires the destruction of those who spread corruption. Al-Shawkani mentions the benefits and purposes in creation, or the recompense for good and evil, or the eventual passing away of all created things.

On the "beautiful forgiveness", opinions differ. Al-Mawardi gives several meanings: turning away without distress, forgiving without rebuke, or accepting without reproach, the last attributed to Ali. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi hold that the verse was abrogated by the verse of fighting, and al-Tabari reports from Mujahid and Ikrima that it came before the fighting was commanded. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi find abrogation unlikely, and Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a consolation for the Prophet.

As for the word "Creator", some readers recite "al-Khaliq"; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that this form suits both few and many creations, while "al-Khallaq" applies mainly to abundance.

God bestows a favour upon His Prophet ﷺ by giving him seven of the mathani and the magnificent Qur'an. For most commentators the seven mathani are the opening chapter, al-Fatiha, which has seven verses and is repeated in every rak'a; they rely on authentic reports in which the Prophet ﷺ said that the Mother of the Qur'an is the seven mathani and the magnificent Qur'an. Among those transmitted from this view are 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra and Ibn 'Abbas. On this reading, mentioning the magnificent Qur'an after the seven is a general term following a specific one. Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan and a number of Successors hold that the seven are the long surahs, from al-Baqara to Yunus or to al-Anfal and al-Tawba, and were called mathani because rulings, punishments, parables and lessons are repeated in them. Tawus, Abu Malik and others say the whole Qur'an is mathani because its stories recur. Others understand the seven as the kinds of discourse in the Qur'an: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, parables, enumeration of blessings and news of earlier nations. Some raise the objection that the surah is Meccan while the long ones are Medinan, and answer that bestowing means sending down to the lowest heaven. The passage then forbids the Prophet to direct his gaze at the worldly comforts given to groups of unbelievers, or to grieve over them, and orders him to lower his wing to the believers, that is, to be gentle and humble with them. Commentators see in this a consolation against the lure of worldly splendour, by means of the Qur'an he has been given.

The commentators explain that this verse tells the Prophet ﷺ not to gaze longingly at the worldly goods given to some unbelievers, not to grieve over their refusal to believe, and to lower his wing gently toward the believers. God has given him the mighty Qur'an and the seven oft-repeated verses, which are far better than what people compete for. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi agree that the verse forbids coveting worldly life and grieving over disbelief, and that lowering the wing means gentleness, kindness and humility, a reading also given by al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud.

The scholars differ on the seven oft-repeated verses. Umar, Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra and most exegetes, including al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, take them to be the opening chapter, al-Fatiha. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid identify them with the seven long surahs, from al-Baqara to Yunus, while Tawus and Abu Malik say the whole Qur'an is meant, and Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam reads them as seven kinds of meaning. On the phrase about the eyes, Ibn 'Uyayna takes it as a call to be content with the Qur'an, whereas Ibn 'Abbas understands it as wishing for what others have.

The "dividers" (al-muqtasimin) are, for Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the People of the Book who split their scripture, and for Qatada and al-Farra', Quraysh who called the Qur'an sorcery, poetry or soothsaying. Some scholars link them to the people of Salih, a view others consider less convincing. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also report several occasions of revelation, though some commentators regard them as weak.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to declare that he is a clear warner, one who alerts people to God's punishment should they persist in denial, just as He sent punishment upon earlier nations. The commentators agree on the explicit sense of warning and on the comparative function of the particle "kamā", though they differ over what object is implied by the act of warning. As for the "muqtasimūn", the views vary: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and Qatāda, in one of their transmissions, understand them to be the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who divided their scripture, believing in part of it and rejecting the rest; al-Farrāʾ and Qatāda take them to be a group of Quraysh who divided the roads into Mecca during the pilgrimage season to turn people away from the Prophet; Ibn Zayd identifies them with the people of Ṣāliḥ who swore to kill him at night; Abū Ḥayyān and others record still other opinions. On the word "ʿiḍīn", Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk take it as the plural of "ʿuḍw", meaning parts and pieces, whereas Qatāda and al-Kisāʾī link it to slander, and ʿIkrima and al-Farrāʾ connect it with sorcery in the dialect of Quraysh. The verse follows the instruction not to grieve over the disbelievers and to lower one's wing to the believers, so the warning confirms the Prophet's mission and announces the fate of those who deny.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to declare that he is a clear warner, and that his warning is like the punishment God sent down upon the muqtasimin. The commentators differ widely on who these were. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, understand them to be the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who believed in parts of their scriptures and rejected others, dividing them up; 'Ikrima reports that some divided the Quran mockingly, saying 'this surah is mine'. Qatada, al-Farra' and others take them to be notables of Quraysh who split the roads into Mecca during the pilgrimage season to turn people away from the Prophet, calling him a sorcerer, a poet or a soothsayer. Ibn Zayd identifies them as the people of Salih who swore to kill him, and al-Akhfash as those bound by oaths. On the word 'idin, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean parts or pieces, while Qatada, 'Ikrima and al-Farra' connect it to slander or to sorcery. The shared point is that those who fragmented the Quran or the Book and described it in contradictory ways deserve punishment, and that the Prophet was not the only one to face such a trial.

God commands His Prophet to declare that he is a clear warner, threatening a punishment like the one sent down on earlier peoples. The commentators differ on who the "muqtasimin" (those who divided) are. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Hasan understood them to be the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who believed in parts of their scripture and rejected others. 'Ikrima reported that they were people who mocked the Qur'an, each saying "this surah is mine". Qatada and Muqatil identified them as Quraysh notables whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughira sent to the roads into Mecca during the pilgrimage season to turn people away from the Prophet, calling him at one point a sorcerer, at another a poet, at another a soothsayer. Ibn Zayd identified them with the people of Salih who swore to kill him by night, a view Ibn Atiyya found hard to reconcile with the phrase that follows. As for "'idin", the plural of "'idah", the best-known reading is "breaking into pieces": they split the Qur'an into fragments and spoke contradictory things about it. Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i linked the word to the root meaning slander or sorcery. Al-Tabari preferred to apply the verse to the polytheists of Quraysh, given the context of the surah. On "By your Lord, We will surely question them all", Abu al-'Aliya and Mujahid took it as a question about the testimony of faith, while others understood it as covering all deeds. God then orders the Prophet to proclaim openly what he is commanded and to turn away from the polytheists, since God is enough for him against the mockers. The passage ends with the command to glorify God, prostrate, and worship until certainty comes, that is, until death.

God swears by His own Lordship that He will question all these deniers on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to do, a questioning that is both rebuke and warning. The commentators differ on the scope of this questioning and on who it concerns. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Zayd hold that it applies to everyone, believers and disbelievers alike, while others take it as directed at the disbelievers and mockers. As for the 'muqtasimun', al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir identify them with the People of the Book who divided their scriptures, believing in some parts and rejecting others, Ibn Kathir citing a hadith in the two Sahihs; al-Farra' and al-Suddi instead identify them with the leaders of Quraysh who divided the roads into Mecca to turn people away from the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and others report that some of them called the Qur'an poetry and others magic. The word 'idin is explained as meaning parts or divisions, or as slander or sorcery according to different lexicographers. All agree the questioning carries the sense of censure and judgment, though they debate the apparent conflict with verse 55:39. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir report from Anas, Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid that the question concerns the testimony 'There is no god but Allah'; Ibn al-Qayyim sees it as sincerity in its fulfilment. The commentators do not firmly decide among these readings.

This verse records a divine oath that God will question all people on the Day of Resurrection about what they did in this world. The commentators explain this questioning in several closely related ways. Most report that it concerns the testimony that there is no god but God, as transmitted from Anas, Ibn Umar and Mujahid; Ibn Kathir and others note that this is attributed to the Prophet through Anas, though some transmit it only as a companion's statement. Abu al-Aliya says that people will be asked about two things: what they worshipped, and how they answered the messengers. Ibn Abbas and those who follow him hold that the affirmed questioning is one of reproach and rebuke rather than inquiry, since God already knows everything; Qutrub adopts this view and distinguishes it from the denied questioning in Surat al-Rahman. Ikrima says the Day has many stations, with questioning in some and not in others. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi extend the meaning to all deeds, whether words, actions or omissions, and al-Qurtubi affirms that the question is general to believers and unbelievers alike, with exceptions for those who enter Paradise without reckoning. Ibn Juzayy reconciles the two verses by distinguishing reproach from pure inquiry. All agree that the verse carries a warning to those who denied the message and divided the Quran into parts.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to proclaim openly what he has been commanded and to turn away from the polytheists without being distracted by their mockery. The commentators explain the verb sadda‘ in several ways. Ibn ‘Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su‘ud take it as making the message manifest and carrying out the command. Mujahid understands it as reciting the Qur'an aloud in prayer. Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjaj, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it as separating truth from falsehood. Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani note that "ma" can be relative, meaning the prescriptions, or verbal, meaning the command itself.

Several commentators report that the Prophet had been concealing his mission until this verse was revealed, after which he and his companions came out openly. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also cite accounts of the revelation's context, which is set against the polytheists' mockery.

On abrogation, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that turning away was abrogated by the verses on fighting, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes that most exegetes agree. Al-Razi, Ibn ‘Atiyya and al-Shinqiti regard this view as weak and hold that the verb means simply to pay no heed to them. Ibn ‘Ashur adds that it concerns their mockery and harm, not their invitation to Islam.

All agree that God sufficed the Prophet against the mockers, and that they perished. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate how five leaders of Quraysh were punished. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa‘di conclude that the verse calls for patience, praise and prayer, and most exegetes take "until the certainty comes to you" to mean death.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet ﷺ, telling him to proclaim openly what he is commanded, to fear none but God, and to turn away from the polytheists without concern, for God has sufficed him against those who mocked him. The commentators agree that the mockers (al-mustahzi'un) were leading men of Quraysh, most of them naming five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib and al-Harith ibn Qays ibn al-Talatila. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir report that they all died before Badr, each struck by a calamity. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and others cite varying accounts transmitted through Ibn Ishaq, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima and Muqatil, which differ on their number and on how each perished. Al-Sha'bi counts seven and includes Habbar ibn al-Aswad, which Ibn 'Atiyya considers a mistake since Habbar embraced Islam on the day of the conquest of Mecca. Al-Razi holds that these details are unnecessary and that it suffices to know they were powerful. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, however, relate the fate of each. As for "until the certainty comes to you", most exegetes, including Ibn Zayd, Mujahid and al-Hasan, understand it as death, while Shajara takes it to mean victory.

This verse states that God sufficed His Prophet ﷺ against those who mocked him. Most commentators name five leading men of Quraysh: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, Abu Zam'a, al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth and al-Harith ibn al-Talatila, who all died before Badr, each through an accident or illness that the reports describe in detail. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi transmit these accounts, while al-Sha'bi and Ibn Abi Bazza speak of seven men, and Ibn Juzayy judges that the likeliest meaning concerns those who died in Mecca before the Hijra, whereas others think of the dead of Badr such as Abu Jahl. The verse then describes them as those who set up another god beside God, and the commentators agree that the final phrase, 'they will know', is a severe threat addressed to every polytheist, with its outcome in this world and the next. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of the command to proclaim openly, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as an order to deliver the message without fear. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that naming the polytheism of the mockers consoles the Prophet by showing that their sin is even graver than their ridicule. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the word 'sawfa' covers several stages, since some enemies later repented, like 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl. The commentaries therefore converge on a clear sense: consolation for the Prophet and a delayed warning to the polytheists.

God tells His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He knows his chest is constricted by what the disbelievers say, whether denial, mockery or attacks on the Qur'an. He commands him to turn to glorifying his Lord with praise, to prostration in prayer, and to keep worshipping until 'the certainty' comes to him, which nearly all commentators take to mean death. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that 'yaqin' means death, citing Salim, Mujahid and Qatada. Ibn Kathir concludes that worship remains obligatory as long as the mind is sound, and he rejects the view that knowledge of God releases a person from duties. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya read the word as the certainty of death rather than death itself, and take the limit to mean the whole span of life; Ibn Atiyya also allows that it may mean the promised victory. Most agree that glorifying with praise is affirming God's transcendence together with thanks, and that prostration means prayer, supported by the report that the Prophet ﷺ turned to prayer whenever a matter distressed him. On the cause of the distress, al-Tabari and others say it is denial, while al-Razi and others say it is mockery; al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the chest here stands for the heart. The verse follows the account of the mockers whom God has sufficed against, and the commentators relate how they died, though their names and number differ between reports.

In this verse, after stating that He knows the Prophet ﷺ is distressed by his people's rejection and mockery, God commands him to turn to his Lord with glorification, praise, and prayer, so that God will suffice him in what troubles him, and to persist in worship until the certainty comes, which the commentators agree means death. Most explain that prostration here means prayer, and that glorification means declaring God free of imperfection together with praising Him. Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that glorifying may be said as “Glory be to God and praise be to Him,” and that those who prostrate are those who pray or who are humble. The majority, following Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, read the certainty as death, while Shajara and Ibn Juzayy, as cited by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to mean the promised victory. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi draw from it the duty to worship as long as the mind is sound, and reject the claim of some mystics that knowledge of God frees one from obligation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that turning to prayer relieves distress, and Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti note that the order to glorify God after the heart’s constriction shows that prayer is a means of removing that burden. Al-Jaza'iri draws from it the legitimacy of prayer for need. Most scholars hold that this verse is not a prostration point for recitation, though some earlier authorities such as al-Naqqash regarded it as one.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to persist in worshipping his Lord until al-yaqin comes to him, which the commentators understand as death. For the majority, the verse means that worship remains obligatory for as long as a person lives, without interruption even for a moment. Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, Salim ibn Abd Allah and Ibn Zayd explain yaqin as death, and al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the report of Umm al-Ala about the death of Uthman ibn Maz'un in support. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Shawkani mention a different reading in which yaqin is the victory promised to the Prophet, a view reported through Shajara and Ibn Bahr. Al-Zajjaj, al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that stating a limit implies continuity, since a bare command to worship could be fulfilled by a single act. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Ashur conclude that the duty lasts as long as the mind is sound, with prayer performed standing, seated or lying down according to one's ability. Ibn Kathir and al-Shinqiti reject as misguided the view that yaqin means knowledge of God, which would lift the obligation of worship. The verse closes a passage in which, after the call to proclaim the message and turning away from the idolaters, the remedy for distress is glorification and prostration, followed by steadfastness in worship until death.
